A WASHINGTON correspondent wrote that "the adjournment of Congress had east a general gloom over the retail liquor business in the nation's capital." A BLACKSMITH in -Nebraska, who chanced to live in a rather irreligious community, put up a sign: "No horses shoed on Sunday, except Sick- and Death." • A DEBATING society is going to discuss the ques- tion, " Was there ever in fact sums an Indian chief as Metamora?" We never mei; a-more a-musing question for debate. A NEVADA editor says that "the red man's style of warfare is too original to be •comprehended by the officers of cur regular army." Ile probably means that it is too aboriginal. YOUNG Spilkins, when he moved into the suburbs and went into the poultry business, soon became discouraged because he conid't find the breed of hens that lay wagers. WE see that -a "house of call in New Jersey is called the "Mosquito Tavern." That must be a place where any hungry wayfarer that stops may be sure of getting a bite. - - "THERE'S a certain fashionable 'church up town," said Dalkins, "that wants a , parishioner with a powerful memory ;—so that he can remember the poor," he 7raintiy added.. A PARTISAN editor declared that the leader of his party was beyond reproach: "yes," said he, "absolutely spotless." "That's so," responded his rival; "there is not a clean spot on him." AN Arizona paper says: "A divorce can be obtained in this Territory by simply jumping over a kitchen poker." The kitchen poker usually. -comes in in quite a different way in divorce mat- ters further east. IsrsPraan by the recent revival ,of " Sweet Home," Mr. Bemus stepped into the house singing —"But give me the piece of mind dearer than all," and Mrs. Bemus gave it so freely that he has'nt called for it since. First Gent.—" Did he, thin? I hope ye hit'm back, suir !" "Does your wife talk in her sleep ?" asked one married man of another One day when they were -comparing notes. " I don't lie awake to see," replied the heartless kusband ; " but she talks all the rest of the time, so I rather guess she does." I wasn't a big donkey when I was of your age." " No ; but you've grown a heap since." But the nights, the long dreary nights must deal out double portions of time?" Convict: "Oh, no. The nights fly faster than the days." Visitor (astounded) : "is it possible ?" Convict: "es. "He did so added the clergyman "and it was not long before every one in the audience mourned over the death of that wife ati that of a personal friend." SOME years ago a lady engaged a domestic ser- vant from the Highlands. In the evening the lady wand supper brought on, so she rang the bell. Getting no answer, she .repeated the summons, but with the same. erect. She then proceeded to the kitchen, where, to her amazement, she found her servant almost convulsed with laughter. She pointed, to the bell and exclaimed, "As sure's I leeve I never touched it, an' it's waggin' yet." He was hurriedly departing when the dealer called after him :—" Hold on, hold on, it's bad ! A statement made to the Eifect that Mr. Glad- stone finished his translation of Horace's odes into English verse on the day that his resignation too plsce is absolutely typical of the Grand Old Man. His power of dissociating ideas even" in the most- pa.ssiOnate moments of his existence has probably never been surpassed, if equalled, by any man placti in such high position. To this, among other circumstances, his continued good health is cer- tainly due. .

Dr..Talmage was announced recently as having decided to resign his pastorate of Brook'yrs Taber- nacle. Various reasons were given, and it was popu- larly supposed that the eminent divine had elected to " accept a call " elsewhere. Reuter has, how- ever, explained the statement in more prosaic language, thus :—" Dr. Talmage has consented to retain his past, the financial troubles caused by the falling off of funds at the Tabernacle having been arranged." •

Mr. Justice McCarthy has been telling a "New Weekly" interviewer an. interesting story about beorge Eliot. " Once," he says, "when I returned from a lecturing tour through America she showed the greatest, interest about life hi Salt Lake City, for at that time Mormonism was at its height. I spoke strongly against the condition of things which prevailed, but I recollect her stiying, in a melan- choly kind of way: Well, married life has not been such a success in the Old World that one can- not look with some interest on an experiment in the New. ' "

By the way, in view of events which may at any moment spring into notoriety, it is interesting to define the exat.t in.aning of the phrase "morgana- tic marriage." Tat) ward is based on the Gothic morgjan,:.which means "to curtail," whence the Low Latin matrimonium ad legem morganatican. It is a I.ort of union permitted to kings and that ilk, but it tried by Brown or Robinson it would lead, on the second attempt to a prosecution for bigamy. The children of such a marriage cannot inherit the title or estates of their father.

A striking proof of the interest taken in Ibsen's remarkable poem, "Brand "—so different in matter and manner from his "social dramas"—is the simultaneous appearance in English 'bf two inde- pendent verse-translations of the work. That by Mr. Garret.`, is now in the press, and will Bhortl3 be pubbshed by Mr. T. Fisher Unwin. Mr. Garrett iP a journalist, and the author of "In_ Afrikanderland,” but has not hitherto published any verse under Iti;, own name. The metres in the translation are said to be those of the original, an effort being made to reproduce even the song of Einar and Agnes in the fir 6t act in rhythm more f4ithful to the original than that of any version yet pubiished.

Many of the Unionist members who have visited their constituencies during the recess have returned with the conviction that the Oppcsition lead6rs mad 4 a tactical mistake in adhering to the principle of nontracting out as regards the Employers' Lia- bility bilL.lt is agreed that in some quarters where the railway interest is strong the principle may have been popular, bur, even in this case there was no support for its application outside existing funds The conviction that a false step has been made in this matter is indeed so strong that. there would be no surprise if after Easter some bill dealing with employers' liability is brought in on the Unionist. benches, in order, if possible, to remove the bad impression caused by the action of the House of Lords. The latest rumour on the Subject is,indeed that such a bill may be brought into the Upper House itself.
This is the way in which that, excellent Conser- vative periodical, the "Liberty Review," speaks of the Duke of Devonshire :7-•

The woke, who has had some experience If politica.; hanky-panky, who had his share inth berrakal et Gor- don.and rtally-scored amazingly by his desertion of Mr. Gladstone, is not absolutely disinclined to listen to sug- gestions tor putting him in command of the coalition vice the Marcinis forcibly resigned—or seconded for ser- vice with the Devil. Remember, once a traitor always a traitor. Be who has once tasted the pleasures of treason can no more forego them than can the dog fore- go that exceedingly unpleasauZ; canine habit referred to by.ing Solomon. From the same organ we learn that the duke chuckles in "his heavy-jowled phlegmatic way," and that Sir Henry Jaynes is his " six-and-eight- penny conscience-keeper."

Two significant rumours are :Current as to the next election of the School Board for London. One is that the election will he fought on political lines so far ai that i possible by the Conservative rnd Church party in the capital ; the other is that Mr. A. Riley, who is at the bottom of all the mis- chief that has discredited .the Diggleite party, is to be thrown overboard to lighten the ship. At any rate, we , may expect some .startling electoral developments before the day of the pont In the meantime the Electoral Council for the Yrogressive party goes _on strengthening itself by an almost dai,ly accession: of influential names. The secre- taries a the Council aro Dr. Cliaord .and Mr. T. Mann—a collocation which .augurs well for unity between the Nonconformist vote and the Labour vote at the election.. bear, further, that among the leaders, of both parties there is a growing im- pression that legislation- will have to be adopte,l in °Tiler to seele the relation of the state to Volun- tary schools in a- way which will, prevent th,- mangling.ancl maladministration which the " w'az of creeds" too often produces at School Board meetings and elections.

it does not appear probable,in spite of the threats which, have been uttered, t hat the House of Lords will go the length of throwing out the Registration Bill on the second reading. They will insist in alter- ing the propolid period of qualification, and will make other changes in the important previsions of thebill. It is pretty certain, too, that they will throw out the " one man, One vote," bill. But the first direct blow which the Upper House is likely to, strike at the Government will be upon the Evicted Tenants Bill, which the Conservative leaders -have evidently made up their minds tb. believe can be rejected without affronting the English constituen- cies, However, it is still to the time of the intro- duction of the Budget that members on both sides are lookink as the period of crisis. So much is this the case that I know that some Liberal members intend visiting their constituencies next week and the week after with the object ef. ensuring that everything shall be in readiness for a possible ;r4eiae.ral election in Nay. -Hitherto it has been mainly tha Conservatives who have been acting on the supposed probability of a general election in the spring; but there can be no doubt that the expecta- tion of an -early dissolution has been spreading in the last few days.

A series of meetings of the Irish majority, ex- tending over threedays, was, brought to a close on Wednesday evening in the Committee-room No: 15. Apart from any questions concerning their organi- zation, the party have been confronted with the complications resulting from a change in the Minis- try, and the situation as been to them one of great anxiety. They have, I hear, decided that for the time being the assurances:received from the Govern- ment as to the future position of Home Rule are hatisfactory,and the support of the party as a whole will thus be given to the Government. The choice 'of the officials of the party occupied a good deal of time, and before the ballot for the committee along discussion took place as to the qualifications of cer- tain new candidates. In the en 4 all the old mem- bers oft he committee were re-elected excepting Mr. A. O'Connor, and in his place LILT. D. Sullivan was appointed. The same result attended the election secretaries so far as Mr. O'Connor was concerned. He was deposed in favour of Mr. William Abraham, who will be the future colleague of Mr. Donal Sulli- van. The sessional Whips will he, as before, Sir. T. Esmonde and Dr; Tanner;but in place of Mr. O'Dris- coll, their assistant, they will have two assistants in the persons of Captain Donelan and Mr. James . Tuite.

The desire to hear Lord Rosebery speak at Edlnburgb on to-day (Saturday) is very great. The Liberal Associa- tion have received a vast number of applications lor tickets; and the meeting, both in size and enthusiasm, promises to equal the memorable gatherings Mr. Glad- stone has _addressed in Midlothian.

It is expected that the coat bodice, which always prevails in some form, will this season ,be especially ohio, and„while not carrying out the idea of the Inoroyable and Direatoire costumes, will yet tend in that direction; and revers of white tiatin or moild will be weei on dark cloth, whilst largo buttons of filisireo and otainped metal will be a fultere on such gamest'.

A useful model for Spriug wear hao-a charming example of a draped skirt, and one peculiarly becoming to a tali, slender fighre. The bAok is gathered, and the bides are raised by pleats which run out tato the waist. Tae foundation is faced to simulate a petticoat of velvet, 'and the top of the bodice lining is also covered Nvlit'Ai velvet to form a yoke, pad this is surrounded by a twist of m silk caught at bei-vals with a fancy buckle.

You will, I expect, admire a mcxidi In multi- coloured homespun. Brown is the predominant shade, flecked with mulberry and green. Cat in tailor style, this bodice ia smartly finished with narrow black braid, edged and intersected with gold thread. Particular attention should be given to the sleeves, which arc beautifully out and well up to date. Lines of the black braid are arranged to follow each seam.

lb seems that plain skirts will be trimmed at the edge, and a very. handsome Parisian model of faille Frangaise in dull fawn has a nine-inch border of moss-green velvet, over which, nob quite reach- ing to the lower edge, came a broad open-patterned guipure in a deep ecru tint. Vandykes of jet, with the straight edge upwards, are used in this same fashion, as, for instance, pale grey silk, green, or darker grey velvet, and jet vandykee. Fashion has seldom been more lenient as regards millinery, and less exacting as to particular styles. Almost any shape is wearable now, but everything must turn up or "tilt," and the tiny toque, or little bonnet, is contrasted by the huge picture hat with feathers standing out in various directions. Now, too, that the hair is worn more flat and cons- pact on top, although still a mass of curls, the turned-up hat is adorned inside with rosettes of satin or jet, or with the very fin-dc-siècle paillette. Most of the models can be trimmed by the amateur milliner, if not completely made at home; but for early spring the made hat of velvet or moire will gradually oust the felt model from popular favour.
A pretty bonnet is in laws itat, with scroll front. It has bandeau and bows of black folded velvet, black tuft and osprey studdth with jet, and steel ornatnents and black strings.

Shot diagonals make up delightfully in the zouave style, and although they are most inexpen- sive yet the effect is smart and dressy in the extreme. For instance, a green diagonal shot with rose, is dark and yet bright, and the zeuave top is edged with vandyke black braid, with dark green spangles. The sleeves are also of the diagonals with frilled epaulettes trimmed with the vandyke braid ; and there is a sleeveless vest and high collar of dull rose erepon, crossed above and down to the bust-Fhe with rows ef spangled braid.
A fee of atventy potinds a day -is giveli the iphysician to the Enipre3s ui ItuiA when iu attenlance upon his august patient.

What a nuisance it must be to possess beautiful dia- monds. Mrs. Helen ButterWorth,uf New York, has had hers stolen, although she was in the habit of placing them in two chamois bags and secreting them in the toes of a pair of walking shoes. She wished to have heavier soles on the shoi lis and her maid was instructed to take them to a shoemaker. The maid believes she must have taken the diamonds to the shoemaker's when she carried the shuesthere for repairs.

Miss Eugenia do Forrest, an actress, who Makes her home in San JosiS, California, has received the sanction of the authorities to wear metes clothes in public, and proposes to obtain a legal right to appear in the same garb ail over the country. She made tier appearance on the streets of San Jose a few days ago in a double breasted sack coat sal waistcoat of dark material,trou- ' sera of a striped patters, and a Derby hat of the latest style. In her 'and she swung an ebony cane. She says she is realising the dream et her life. She is tired of skirts, aria as her stage appearances are mostly in Male parts she knows the greater comfort of male attire. , The paper on which letters to the Queen Victoria are written must not be folded. No communication which bears evidence of having been creased will ever fall into, Her Majesty's own hands: The proper method is to Write onthick glossy white paper, and to despatch the missive in tti envelope which fits it. Any folded oom- tounication never reaches the Queen, for the simple reason that she won't look at it. Alt such letters are opened by the Mistress of the Robes, and as a:rule their contents never get beyond her; or, if the letter is of im- portance, it is returned tothe writer with the directions hot., to forward it.

The tiny, slender; pretty wife of the Crtr, says Mr. Joseph Hatton, likes to think that she shields her hus- band from the Nihilist conspirators. Danger has a cer- tain weird charm :tor her. She enjoys risking her life to share her husbands peril, in riding on horseback to reviews with him, and in always being by his side when driving. She is intensely jlalout of her moral influence over het children. Nobody must share that responsi- bility. She does nA permit them to have governors or governesses, only teachers. These go to their duties In rotation ;there is the English teacher to-day,the French to-morrow, the German the day after and so en, and no time is given any of them to gain the ascendency over their pupils.

div.head: Repairing Nerve Tissue.
div.p: Repairing Nerve Tissue.

Dr. Andrew Wila-ou sa-ys he, recently happened to be dining alone with a well-known shrgserA in Lusy prac- tice. His friend was a man who, like himself, purnevs over the length and breadth of the land. He bad just returned from a long and tedious journey, tired and fagged. They sat down to dinner. Between the courses the surgeon fell sound asleep, let us say, ter three mM- utes—not more certainly. After each nap he woke up, ate his quantum. and IV'ent-dff agaia intb slumber. Dr. Wilson said nothing, but watched him closely. I.h. observed tat after each awakening the surgeAl grew brighter,the tired look disappe,,red, and by the time din- ner was at an 'end Richard was himself again. Dr. Wil- son joked him on his instalmenti of sleep. His rep;y Was characteristic. " Don't you know," he said," tlia,' it isn't a long sleep which is needed to refresh an active brain? Nerve-tissue is repaired . easily With very little sleep if you also take food."
The Hair. 1

It goes without saying that the management of the hair is a very important factor in personal appearanceli A French lady (the Baroness,Staffe) asks : " Is there, a- woman living y/bo has not coveted the mantle of a king' sung by Musset ? • • " Ce,te Chevelure qui l' inonde, Plus longue qu' on manteau de mi.' - And in truth it is a splendid ornament which nature has bestowed on her chosen ones, and which they ought to ,know how to preserve—as, indeed, every one ought, no. -matter what kind of hair they have been given. Oi course, to be really beautiful,. hair should be abundant, fine, and brilliant. lilt let not those despair altogether whose hair is thin, short, coarse, or lustreless I These faults may be somewhat, if not a great deal, diminishq, by intelligent efforts. But all the beautiful qualities we have enumerated will tiot suffice for many women. It Weir. hair is black .as a raven's wing, they want to bt fair,as all, nearly all, the•fatal and fascinating women. of history have been. Eve, they saY,was fair as honey, ; the locka of Venus streathed over her divine shoulder:, in a golden flood; the hair of Ceres was the,colour of the harvest; Helen the beautifiil, whom even the old men of Troy could not,see without emotion, crowned her:ador- 'able hsad with fair hair like ripe corn. Salome, who asked for and obtained the head of John the Baptist, had yellow hair—rat least the old masters paintmd her fair, like the young Jewel-se.4 of high birth. Luci.etia Berg,ia. Lady Macbeth, and Queen ,Mary, were ad blondes ; Queen Dizabetit had red flair ; Catherine and Maria d,- 201edicis were also fair. .The colour of the hair depern4s chiefly upon its chemical constituents. These are com- bined with the natural oil „substance conttined in the hair tubes in varying proportions—carbon, hydrbgeh , nitrogen, oxygen, sulphur, &c. Red hair contains iron;. white or grey hair, phosphate of magnesia and phosph- ate of lime, and little or no sulphur or iron.; black hair is liberally supplied with iron, which ceases to be present much earlier than the sul'eliur, and for this reason 'dark hair usually turns grey sooner than the lihei colours.

A big bed- room, well Ventilated is a necessity. Sponging is what is recommended, also getting as much fresh air as possible. WEBOTRIL

We will now take the rtader behind the scenes which the earl and Lord. Ai-114yr° would have 'given so much to penetrate. The Lady Beatrice hurried from the drawing- room to her own apartments, of which a description has already been given. A soft mellow light flooded the entire suite, and an even summer heat pervaded the air. The curtains were all drawn, and an easy-chair stood conveniently near to the fire. A moorish cushion in front of the chair up- held a pair of dainty scarlet velvet slippers, and over the carved chair-back was thrown carelessly a white dreszsing-gown whose scarlet silk lining looked like the red reflection of the flaming coals. . The Lady Beatrice pranced about the rooms, as if in search of some one who was not there, and then touched her bell-pull. Her face was flushed with annoyance at the re- memberance of her recent interview with Lord Adlowe ; her- manner full of agitation. She was angry at herself for her final evasion of his pro- posals of marriage, and she moved across the floor once or twice like a caged lioness, murmur- ing " The insufferable creature! How dare he look at me in that manner? For the moment I was pos- itively afraid to anger him. He would be a dan- gerous enemy, I fear. I must conciliate him by pretending to consider his suit, and perhaps some- thing may occur to relieve me of his perse- cutions.' - She paused, as her door opened, and her per- sonal attendant appeared in answer to her sum- mons.

This attendant was a woman past middle age severe of aspect, with a countenance expressive of marked fidelity and truthfulness. That she was devotedly attached to her beautiful mistress was evident at the first glance. She had lived with her many years and served, her in the capacity of tire-woman and seamstress, being in reality a lady's maid without. the name. Unlike a lady's maid, she spent but little time in the apartment of her mistress, and hence had never been ques- tioned or suspected of knowing anything in regard to the mysterious seclusions Of the Lady Bea.tTice. She had little in common with the family servants and spent most of her time in her own room, which was bituuted conveniently near to those of her lady. "Dress me quickly, Fleck,".said the Lady Bea- trice' glancing at her pretty ormolu clock. "I have only fifteen minutes to spare."' She began stripping off her bracelets, rings and necklace, tossing them in a glittering heap upon a lace-draped dressing-table. "The night is very wild, my lady," said the tire- woman; in a tone of remonstrance. "Do you hear the storm ? " _ _

The wind-dished past the Windows uttering a wild wail that was inexpressibly mournful. "I hear it," said , the Lady Beatrice, "but I do not heed it. There is a storm wilder than that in my. heart. I must. go out, Mary. Do not try to dis- suade me." Mrs. Flock made no reply. She approached her mistress, disengaged the brooch that sparkled at her throat, removed her laces and unbuttoned the ruddy velvet robe, letting it fall in a confused heap. The Lady Beatrice hastly tossed it into the nearest closet.

" )Tow the out-door- ch'ess 1" said her ladyship. The tire-woman brought from a hidden corner of the wardrobe, a plain, humble-looking grown, of serge, brown in line, and destitute of trimming. Her ladyship donned it, and buttoned the corsage over her magnificent bnMi.. "Now my boots," she said, Oinking into a chair, and extending her delicately slippered, feet. The tire-woman , brought heavy Walking-boots, small and well-shaped,- but of leather that accorded well with the dress the Lady Beatriee had assumed. They laced them about the shapely ankles with sin- gular quickness. "My cloak!" Mrs. Fleck produced a long, thick, waterproof cloak that reached to the hem of her ladyship's dress, and wrapped it about her mistress. There was an upper cape . that effectually concealed the outlines of the Lady Beatrice's majestic figure. When the lady's head had been enshrouded in an old-fashioned bonnet of considerable proportions, her face covered with a veil, and she had taken a. cotton umbrella in her hand; the disguise was com- plete. She seemed an . elderly woman whom poverty compelled to brave the rough weather. " Theie, that will do," said her ladyship, her voice sounding muffled throuali thethickbrown veil, which she had doubled over her face. "The doors are all locked, Mary. Turn' down the gas 'a little. Now come and let me out." . •

Mrs. Fleck conducted her disguised mistress through the rooms of the site, into the bathroom. Proceeding to a closet adjoining the bath, she entered it, opened a door in its back wall, which was cleverly concealed by the garments that hung against it. Passing through the aperture of the sitting room into an ante-room that served as a sleeping- chamber.
The lady Beatrice followed into her tirewoman's chamber.

The door leading into the closet was concealed on this side, as on the other, by a multitude of hang- ing garments. The tire-woman turned the key in the lock and Withdrew it, depositing it in a closet near at hand.
" You have your pass-key, my lady ? " she asked.

"Yes. I shall probably not be at home till to- morrow evening. I shall return in time to dress for dinner, as I always do. Conie. I have no more time to spare." qhey issued from the tire-woman's chamber into the corridor, Mrs. Fleck pausing to lock the door behind them. She then hastened into the rear por- tion of the mansion, conducting her mistress, down the servants' staircase into the basement corridor, from the sides of which opened the servants' hall, the offices and similar rooms. The corridor was deserted, and but dimly light- ed. Sounds of merriment issued from the serv- ants' hall, but the Lady Beatrice did not heed them. She was not even startled when the door opened, and one of the men-servAnts looked out, inquiring: "Is that you, Dick? Here we • are a-waitin' for

you-7' " Tan't Dick," said the tire-woman, in an un- moved voice. "It's me—Mrs. Fleck—and my poor old aunt." "Ah 1 your poor old aunt ! " said the man, with a mocking bow at his disguised mistress. "The old lady hangs on well, Mrs. Fleck: she's been here at least once a week for these fiteen years. I wish I had a relative as thought as much of Me." He shut the door, and a great shout of laughter came from the servants' hall. Evidently the foot- man was impa:rting to his social equal i some ex- quisite witticism concerning Mrs. Fleck's ancient relative. . The Lady Beatrice quietly followed her guide to the area door, and then parted from her, ascending the area steps into the street. She passed her own lighted drawing-room windows, behind the curtains of • which her fathee_and Lord Adlowe sat

n conversation. She hurried along through the gloom and tempest, protected from the elements by her cloak and umbrella. The fitful light of the gas lamps flickered through the watery atmosphere, scarcely revealing to the few whom she met her hurrying shape. .After a brisk walk of several minutes she arrived at Victoria station. A throng of reople was moving in the same direction as herself. She lost herself among them passing up the broad stairways to the platform, before which the train stood ready for departure. A guard, with consideration for her supposed age and physical infirmities, assisted her into a second-class coach, for which grade of carriage she displayed a yearly ticket, slammed the door upon her, and departed to attend to some apparently younger and wealthier passenger. The Lady Beatrice shrank into her corner with a feeling of relief, the whistle sounded, and the train glided from the station. It was a strange adventure for ai delicately nur- tured lady, that night-ride in a second- einA. enr- riage, with its meagre furnishings and its dim light, with the heavy ram beating against the windows. and with the wild March wind screaming through the air. And yet it did not seem strange to tile, Lady Beatrice. She was evidently in the habit of making these singular excursions, and in her present disguise. , She sat silent and immovable, grasping the knob of her umbrella in her cotton-gloved hands, her humble attire. The other passengers exclaimed I - Paguatt_tht Irtnacnt fitcuuta 91 tau tau. LL hsj
was impatieut, she did .not betray it by •.vorti gesture.

- At length, when several miles had been tr;;;To.sed, and the train had paused at a small country stati,mt the Lady I.latrice aligted from the coach. There were few people on the platform. She pa.rcd three, descended the stairs, and inAde her way iiito the btreet.

It was raining drearily as ever. A sill glo gas lamp reveaied one or two antiquated eat.; waiting for c4alce passengers. She looked r.t both, as if ex:rx)eting to sell a third vehicle, and murnmro.d : "They do not expet me to-might. Tnny think I dare not venture out." . She heEitateui a mornezt, and one of the cabmen approached, goliciting her uotrona%ge. She immedi- ately engaged him, a iolv• it wt. conducted to his vehicle.

"Where to, madam ?" asked the man, closing the door, and holding up the strap of the window. "To the Evergreens !" replied the Lady Bea- trice; in a voice that was strangely in keeping with her assumed character.
"The Evergreens! Oh, that is the Sr,tnish cOunt's place. All right mum." And thc closed the window, and mounted to his box.
The next in:Dtant he cracked his whip, the horse started, and the Lady Beatrice was being borue to her destination.

It was a ride of full fifteen mintes, over a coun- try road. There were little villas scattered along on either side of the road, each standing in its own small garden, and each bearing agrand and sonorous title. There were occasional gas-lamps gleaming like fire-flies through the rain and mist, but they shed no light on the dismal scene. " Almost there!" breathed the Lady Beatrice, wiping the damp from the window with the back ef her glove, and peering into the gloom. The villas nqw occurred at less frequent intervals, and, as well as could be ascertained in the darkness, the vehicle had gained the open country. The time we have indicated above as the duration of the journey had but little more than transpired, when the cab stopped before a spot of denser blackness at one side of the road, and the driver alighted and opened the door, saying: • "Here you are, mum. This is the Evergreens, You can't see the house, mum 'cause of the thick, green trees, but it's back there a ways, a hidden as 'twere. Jest you ring at the garden door, mum, and some null let you in, I make no doubt." He assisted her out of the vehicle, but made no offer to ring :for her. Evidently h. not in the habit of wasting Much attention MA elderly and humbly dressed women. The Lady Beatrice paid him, an Int tea quietly in the direction of the garden doom, *with whose position long experience must have made her familiar, for she could not distinguish it in the darkness. The cabman mounted his box and drove back in the direction whence he had come. The disguised belle produced a . key from the pocket of her cloak, and moved it cautioiisly over the face of the, of the door. It sank into the lock. She turned the bolt, withdrew the key, -Opened the •door, and passed within, locking the door behind her.

_ It was a long and wide shrubbery in which she found herself, a regular plantation of pines and firs and Norway sprdees, all of which were well grown and thickly interlaced. Au irregular path ran like a serpent among the trees, approaching the house in such a roundabout manner as not to com- mand a view of it from any point.

The Lady Beatrice elevated her umbrella to keep off the rain that dripped from the surcharged branches and walked- along the dark path. A more timid woman would not have dared take that lonely night walk between those grim rows of trees in that gloomy, labyrinthine walk, but her ladyship neither sighed nor murmured at her task. She walked with a quick, springing step, as one ap- proaches a great happiness. The labyrinth was threaded at last, and the Lady Beatrice came out in front of a beautiful cottage orinSe large enough to have been termed a villa. it was 'blazing with light. Great bay windows, with lace and silken drapiers, looked like gigantic shaded lanterns. Music floated out softly, sweetly, faintly, like the echoes of a dream. Voices and laughter came in dim snatches to the visitor's ears.

"They did not exp eet me to- n ight," she murmured, • unconsciously repeating the words she had used at. the station. "I will give them a pleasant sur- prise." She glided around to a small side porch against a portion of the house less brilliantly lighted. Producing a second key, she opened the door that gave from it. Leaving her umbrella outside, she shook her wet garments and paased into the dWell- ing,fuading herself in a narrow and 'add oin used passage. Opening a door at the 'side *of this passage, the Lady Beatrice disclosed a flight of private stairs. She ascended these. cautiously, almost noiselessly. They terminated at the top upon a narrow landing, from which opened two rooms. One of these, a bath-room, the disguised lady entered. There Was a dim light burning, enough to reveal the tesselated marble floor and the marble bath in the corner. The Lady Beatrice looked the door by which she had effected an entrance, and tore either veil, hood, and cloak, tossing them upon a chair. She then removed her muddy boots anti damp dress, and, half nnrobed and shivering with cold, she cautiously °paned the door /of the adjoining room, looked in, and followed her glances with her person. It was a simple, pleasant little dressing-room in which she found herself, with crimson carpet, long crimson curtains, a soft light, and red tongues of flame shooting up from the bed., of coals in the grate. The Latiy Bcal,rice warmed herself, and then proceeded to an adjoining closet, bringing forth articles of apparel, in which she proceeded to robe her. pen rso, al4;ting as one who had the rights of a Mistress and proprietress.

She .was no longer- the icy and haughty Lady Beatrice, A subtle smile gave sweetness to her rare mouth; her glorious eyes seemed to hold stars within ,their glocmy depths. She attired herself in softly flowing skirts, black satin slippers, aad a dress of AVarm-colouted silk, infinitely becoming her brunette beauty. A simple lace collar edged fhciteek of her robe, anddrills of lace fell like mist lnut her Wrists. Her attire was simple, not costly,. yet not unworthy. Olher..

_ . A woman of moderate income might have worn her present attire at Imam ant not appeared over- dressed. But the Lady Belltrie wore it as a queen might have worn her royal robes, and seemed to delight in its disiwilarity to the attire she had worn at an earlier heur of ,the evening. She wore no jewels, no ornaments. There was a splendidly pail:4(A portrait of herself upon the wail, and before the picture stood a little carved table bearing only a vasie of fresh and edorons . flowers. ,The Lady Beatrice noticed the delicate compliment implied in the offering to her pictured semblance, ,and gathered from the vase a white. camelia, Which . she fastened among • her jetty

braids. "Now I will go down she said softly, smiling as none of thelashionable world had ever seen the Lady Beatrice Hampton smile—a sweet, clear light leaping to her eyes. " How surprised they will be!" _ _
(To Ir continued).

Bennet, whose hus- band posted her in the newspapers, and then had the impudence to run away with anothor woman, returns the compliment in the following spirited manner, through the columns of the Woonsocket paper :—" As ne one would have trusted him for as much as a peck uf meal, I therefore forbid any, person or persons trusting him on my account, as I shall pay no debts of his ,contracting after this date. I have worked to 'support him in gambling and laziness as long as I mean to, although, should he die soon, I will pay the funeral expenses with pleasure."

TuE NATIONAL ANTHEM AS A DEATH SONG. Lord Gifford, V. 0., communicat-is the 'following to Reuter's Agency :—The Ehin. Ma,urics Gifford writes by this mail a graphic account of how Mljor Wilson and his party met their fate in their plucky attempt to cap- tureLobengula. Mr. Gifford obtained the information from a:lin:tuna of the Insuka Ittgiment, who was pre- sent at the engagement. Tua account is briefly as follows : -

On Major Wilson and his party returning with C %Wain Borrow's reinforcements to the King's scnerna in the morning, they were received by a volley frnn p i,rt of the Inguba and fmbisu Regiments, who hal orders te take up their position on the road by which Major Wilson and his party would return. On receiving the volley Majer Wilson retired into the bush towards the river, but he found his party surrounded on all sides by natives, numbering from 2,500 to 3,000 at the very leapt- The orders from the Indunas to their men were that on reaching Major Wilson's party they were to shoot the horses first. This order the Matabele proceeded to carry into effect, Major Wilson's party keeping up a heavy fire' all the time. The horses, which Major Wilson had tied together in a ring, were soon all shot. The Beglishmen then lay dovin behind them, and kept up a steady flee, with suet) good effect that they succeeded in driving off the Matabele for a short time, but reinforcements arriv- ing from across the river the attack was again renewed and, as far as Mr. Gifford could gather from the Induna, the fight Must have lasted some three hours.. A number of our men were seep to be wounded, and their ammu- nition began to run short. Then the natives gradually , crept up closer, shooting anyone they could. The Induna, describes Major Wilson most accurately by his dress and the hat he wore, and states that he was wounded in several places and covered with blood,' whilst another wounded man stood by his side loading rifles and handing them to him. Major Wilson and his men fought desperately to the very Last. Mr. Giffprd adds that, knowing Wilson as he and those associated with him did, as a man of high courage and dstermirra;- tier', he could not imagine him doing other than selling. . his life dearly. The Induna said that as the supreme moment came,the Englishmen who were still able to rise stood shoulder to shoulder, took off their hats, and - joined in a song, the kind of song that he (the Induna) bad heard missionaries sing to the natives. The Mata- bele then rushed up, and whilst the men were singing , what we suppose to have been "God Save the Qeeeni,” they were overwhelmed by the matives and assenied. The Induna estiMated that the Matabele lost eight bo every one of the thirty-four white men killed, and said, that Lobengula's warriors lay round the dead men like grass. _ _
- It has beconv!known that the King had left his camp half-ara-hour before Major Wilson's party arrived opposite the seherrn whion surrounded it.
OIL PAINTING BY THE YARD.
A. representative of " Cassell's Saturday Journal " gleaned some interesting particulars the other day from an artist concerning his profession and the retnuneration
he received:—

" I suppose you make a decent living out of the work ?" was the first question put. For answer the artist handed for his querist's inspection an order he had received that morning from a certain firm. The order was for twelve dozen oil paintings—twelve ioches by eight inches, at fourponce each—the artist to find his own boards and oils. Payment was to be made once:a month, and the following conditions were affixed Five per cent, discount, the work to be executed within • fourteen days and sent home securely packed. The paintings to be assorted—two thirds landscapes and one- third marines as per samples. Specimens of the latter to be submitted. "Great powers !" exclaitned the re- presentative, " but surely this is a joke." " Unfortun- ately, no," said the artist wearily ; " I have tried most of the firms that I know, and those terms are as good as ' I can obtain elsewhere." "And how long .will it take you to execute the order ?—it only represents £2 Bs. altegether." "I shall have to work closely to finish the ' job in the specified time. 'This pay is good compared O, .that of the ppm* girls who work indoors. I know lotsof•, female artists who work ten hours a day—six.clays a week—and earn only ten or twelve shillings. I know • one place where oil paintings are done by the yard'. How ? lii tell you : A. great length of canvas is stretched out and marked into lengths—varyirr in size, :‘,',o='• of course, according to the dimensions of the required picture. Suppose, for instance, a landscape is wanted, ' several artists are engaged, and tach fills in a certain part. One, for instance, will fill in the 'skies, one after , the other, all along the canvas. No. 2 puts in the foli- age, No. 3 the water, and No. 4. will touch up' the whole—laroducing perhaps a figure or two. The can- . vas is then divided into pictures, which are sold as genuine oils. Mounted in cheap heavy-looking gilt frames, they sell fast enough. Tho rate of pay is en „ low that toe workmanship of a picture—say eighteen , inches by twenty-two inches—does not exceed tWe'-' shillings." "Do you think that such as these are fivief . • palmed off as the work of competent painters ?" "'ref!, certainly they are in the provinces ; and I believe also' la some parts of London. The, travelling auctioneer who, • , visits a town for a week or so can .get rid of almort any number of them." • .

div.head: ANOTHER BURNLEY MIRACLE.
div.p: ANOTHER BURNLEY MIRACLE.
"I COULD HARDLY CRAWL."'
(From the Burnley Gazette.)

A case even more remarkable in some of its features than.the one which recently attracted so much attention in Burnley, is just now, says the Burnley Gazette, in everybody's mouth. It relates to the experience of an aged woman living at 16, River-st., and the reports con- cerning it were of such an extraordinary nature that a reporter from the Burnley Gazette was led to make full inquiries into the affair. He found the old lady enjoy- ing her mid-day meal with her husband, Mr. dames Rimtner, and the evident satisfaction with which they took up the subject showed that they were under a deep sense otgratitude for the wonderful change effected in her condition.
*" She has done more work this week," said the hus- band, ". than she has done in the whole course of two years."

"Yes," said Mrs. Rimrner, "I shall never be tired of telling of my restoration from misery to health. For two years and more I've been racked with rheumatic pains, which have almost completely taken away the use of the left leg. Indeed, I have scarcely been able to move about the house all that time. It's been as much as' could do to potter about the house now and again with a stick in one hand; or else clinging to the table and the other furniture as I crawled along. I couldn't even get across the floor without holding on to something, like this," and suiting the action to the word, she got up from her seat and showed our interviewer how she used to crawl from her chair to the cupboard, when trying to do a little towards making tea.

"If I attempted to wring out a few clothes," she con- tinued, "I should be distracted with pain in five minutes, and be forced to lie down in agony. Week after week I have had to lie up nearly all the time with my leg stretchad out in front of me, altogether helpless."

," Were you never able to ge) out oi the house ?'' , "Now and again I managed to get into a neighbour's house, but I had to walk with a stick in one hand and cling ,to the wall with the other, and it was very pain- ful toot

"But you appear'ag well as ever now, and people are saying that a miracle has been done—the lame made to walk. Did you take any medicine during your illness "Yes, all sorts of things; but if the pain in my leg was relieved at night it was as bad as ever next day." , " Well, how was the miracle effected ?"

"I happened to read in the papers," said the husband, "about a case of rheumatism they had cured at Brad- ford by a new scientific remedy,Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and I thought they would just suit my wife's complaint." Mrs. Itimmer went on to describe the er.straordinary results produced by this remedy. She started taking Dr. Williams' Pink Pills a fortnight ago, and had only taken just over a box, at the time of the interview. "I had only had four pills," she said, "when I began to feel they were doing me good. the pain was very much less, and I was feeling better in every way. Before the end of the week the pain had gone entirely out of my leg, and I hi:l4e never had a single ache since. Dr. Wil- liams' Pink Pills have made a new woman of me, and I shall never be afraid of telling anybody. I can work about the house now as I did years since before the rheu- matism tame on."

To corroborate her story Mrs.Rhnmer jumped up from her seat and marched across the room with wonderful agility for a woman of 72. "The neighbours," she continued, "were surprised to see me out this week without a stick, which I haven't been able to do for more than two years. One of them said, There's something funny about this : it is a modern mi'racle.' Another one asked me if I was start- ing my young days over again, and I certainly feel a good many ycars younger." Mrs. 'thinner went on to say that her appetite had greatly improved, that she could sleep soundly at night instead of beingtacked with pain, and also that the swelling of her body, which had troubled her for a long time, had also gone away. She ascribed her recovery solely to Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. The above story was vouched for by a number of the nebighbours who were interviewed by the reporter, who had been instructed to verify the case in the most rigid manner.

Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale • People are also a per- fect blood builder and nerve restorer, curing luch dis- eases as rheumatism, sciatica, neuralgia, partial paralysis, 1,..•,0mct1r ataxy, St. liitu3 &ince, nervous headache, nervous rrostration, and the tired feeling resulting therefrom, diseaacs depending upon humour in the blond, such as scrofula, chronic erysipelas, &c• Dr. Williams' Piuk Pills restore pale and sallow com- plexions to the glow of health, and are a specificfor all the troubles peculiar to the female sex, while in the case of men they effect a radical cure in all cases arLiing from mental worry, over-work, or excesses of whatever nature.

These Pills are manufactured by the Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, of 45, Holborn Viaduct, London, England, and are SOH by chemists everywhere (but only in boxes with pink wrapper bearing the full 'name, Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People) at 2s. 91. a troc, or six boxes for 133. 9d. They may be had direct by post from the Company at the same price. Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People are never sold in bulk, or bv* the dozen or hundred, and any dealer who offers substi- tutes in this form is trying to defraud, and should be avoided.'

SELT:4 DIRECTORY OF RFOISTEIEI9 TELEGRAPIITC AD- DRESSES. —There has just been published by Sell's Adver- tising Agency. London, another adclition to their excel- lent " DirectAry of Registered Telegraphic Addresses," which has been revised and amply supplemented from official lists specially supplied under licence of the post- master-Gt,neral. To commercial men this book, even in its first volumes, proved to be valuable beyond compu- tation ; and there is no doubt that this, the eighth edition, comprehensively amplified as it has beenovill be still more useful and valuable. It will he remembered that Mr. Sell, the publisher oi the work,commenced this compilation in consequence of the widespread dissatisfac- tion felt among commercial rien at not being able to get information from the Post Office as to the senders of tele- grams when signed by a Registered Code Word, and also as to what was the Coda Word of the firm with which they wished to communicate. In supplying this want, Mr. Sell must have earned the gratitude of the commer- cial men of the country.

div.head: NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH
div.p: NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH
CHOIR.

The Town Hall, at Earlestown, was on Thursday evening nicely filled with an appreciative audience on the occasion of a COncert,' given by Mr. H. H. Pearson, ot Warrington, in aid of the funds of the choir connected with the Newton Congregational Church. The concert was really organised by Mr. Thomas Thompson, and Mr. W. H. Thompson, who have worked energetically to ensure success, and their efforts have no doubt been rewarded by a substan- tial addition to the choir funds. Certainly in a musical sense the concert was a success, although it must be admitted that the programme embraced items, which are not generally submitted to Earlestown audiences. This of course is not due to any lack of appreciation on the part of the audience, but rather to an error of judg- ment on the part of the caterers. Mr. Pearson and his Warrington friends submitted a programme on this occa- sion which from first to last was thoroughly enjoyable. Opening with a trio for piano,violin and cello a"Rondo" from Haydn and " Coombe " Gounod, by Messrs. Ford Pearson, and Bond, which was artistically played. Mr. Fieldhouse gave a fine interpretation of the nauti- cal song "The Lanshoreman," but he appeared to much better advantage us his second song " Star of tho desert,'.' with violin ohligato, by Mr. Pear- son, and for this he received a recall, repeating the last verse. Miss Thompson in the song" Good-bye," was in capital voice, and she did full justice to the song ; she was deservedly encored and gave "Robin Adair." Her best effort perhaps was in "The Gift," which she sang in a voice full of pathos, and for this she as also recalled. Miss Thompson is too seldom seen on local concert plat- forms. A duo piano and violin from "Lucia di Lammermoor," was cleverly executed by Messrs Ford. and Pearson. Mrs. Pearson gave a very careful inter- pretation Of that beautiful song "The Holy City," and in response to a recall, she gave "When the children are asleep." Her other item was "The flight of ages," which Was suitably acknowledged. In tbe song "Once Again," Mr. W. Howard 'was fairly successful, hut he showed some improvement in "The Last Watch." although a somewhat more difficult song. Mr. T. R. Ford proved himself a capable musician, and was able to discourse some delectable music on the much abused concertina, his contribution being "Blue Bells of Scot- land," with variations, and he received a recall, which he responded to. The second part of the programme was opened with a trio for piano, violin and cello, andante and allegretto, from Meudelssohn's "Hymn of Praise," which Messrs. Ford, Pearson and Bond, sub- mitted with excellent taste. The same players also gave a trio later on of a" more racy character, " Intemezza " and "Caprice," which was much enjoyed. The humour was supplied by Mr. Haynes, Warrington, whose amus- ing contributions were " Influenza "and "The Waiter," and were rendered in the artiste's inimitable style, with, of course, the usual encores. Mr. W. H. Thomp- son accompanied on the piano, with his accustemed

div.head: ST. HELENS ELOPEMENT.
div.p: A ST. HELENS ELOPEMENT.
A WARRINGTON MAN IMPLICATED.

The gossips of Greenbank and St. Helens were, says a Liverpool contemporary, on Monday, discuss- ing a choice piece of scandal caused by the disap- pearance of two parties, a man and a woman. The man hailed from Warrington, and the woman was the wife of a St. Helens collier. The man had bee% employed by Messrs. Clarke, of ;.-It. Helens and Prescot, general dealers, his occupation principally consisting of the somewhat nomadic lite of getting up odds and ends in town and country. 4e also lodged on. the Crescnt, and appears to have becine enamr4ured of the collier's wife. There was also a young woman lodging with the latter, and the n&ghbours thought the visits referred to this person. The parties concerned, including the hus- band of the runaway, have frequently been to the People's Palace and theatre together, and everything appeared perfectly straightforward until Saturday night, when the lover and the wife were missing. The other inmates stayed up until a late hour, and all inv.iries were made, but without avail. The woman had taken her two children and some money. The only conclusion the husband could arrive at,was that the missing couple had eloped, and on Monday morning he started in search of them, but so far none of the parties have turned up.

div.head: NAVAL PROGRAMME.
div.p: THE NAVAL PROGRAMME.
GREAT INCREASE OF EXPENDITURE.

The Admiralty issued on Thursday night a statement explanatory of the Navy estimates for the coming year. 'rho amount required is £17.366.100, or £3,126,000 more than the sum votod for 1393-4. This large initreaso is duo to shipbuilding, armaments, manning, victualling, new works, and royal navy reserves. 'fho numl,er of seamen, marines, and stokers, is to be largely increased; iiad new works of an extensive character are to be pri- vided at the British dockyards, and also at Gibralter and Malta. Special attention is being, paid to the provision of torpedo boat destroyers. With reference to the new programme Lord Spencer says it is proposed to commence seven battle ships of the first class, six cruisers of the second class, and two sloops. The main features of the new battle-ships will follow generally the designs of the Majestic and Magnificent, now being constructed at Portsmouth and Chatham respectively. And it is pro- posed to build five of them in dockyards—two at Ports- mouth, two at Chatham, and one at Pembroke.

div.head: • 111 E 14: KA M.INER, SATURDAY, MARCH 17, 1894. CIIARGE AGAINST A WARRINGTON POLICEMAN.
div.p: • 111 E 14: KA M.INER, SATURDAY, MARCH 17, 1894. CIIARGE AGAINST A WARRINGTON POLICEMAN.

At the Warringt,rm Borough Court, on Tuesday, Constable John Turner was charged with having on the 9, h inst., unlawfully assaulted and beaten Win. Donoghue. Mr. W.ll..T.Rukins prosecuted and Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. Mr. Jen- kins in opening the case said the complainant. Wm. Donoghue worked tor the Tanner's-lane Tanning Company. On the Friday previous at a quarter past, seven Donoghue went to visit his sweetheart at her mother's house in Brown's-yard,off Winwick-st. lle remained there until shortly before ten o'clock. On going home he met a 111 rs. Cotton who had also been in the same house, and asked her for some money for tobacco which was given him. P.C. Turner with another constable in plain clothes met Donoghue, and Turner asked him " Who is that woman you were talking to." Before he had time to reply, Turner with a stick struck him a very violent blow on the face,caus- hig blood to flow. Donoghue then went to Mrs. Cotton's house accompanied by the two officers, where he washed • his face. fie told them at the house that Turner had done it, but Turner denied that he had done so. He was taken to the Infirmary where his wounds were dressed. The following morning ho applied for a summons to the magistrates which was granted without any hesitation. Donoghue accompanied by his brother went into Mr. Hunt's *office when the summons was handed to P.C. Turner. A conversation took place in which Donoghue told Turner that he was the man that struck him across the nose with a stick. Tur- ner denied it and said a man whoyeas passing Donoghue at the time struck him. The (Thief Constable then told Turner that if he saw a man strike him why didn't he take him into custody. That was unexplained, and he (Mr. Jenkins) contended there was no truthfulness in it. He could not concAve whatever could have caused Turner to strike this man such a violent blow wills a stick with- out the slightest provocation. . If it was an error, if it was an accident he would rejoice to hear that explana- tion given. Win. Donoghue corroborated his solicitor's statement and said there was only one blow struck. There were no other people in the street at the time, and by the aid of the liht from the Bavhorse Inn, he was able to see whe struck him. He was sober at the time.

Mrs. Cetton deposed to giving the complainant lid. for some tobacco at 10.10 in the street. A few minutes after- wards he returned to her house with his face bleeding. The 10. was still in his hand. He told her that Turner had due it. She then told Turner it was a shame for him to (1,) it, hut Turner " stuck to it " that he didn't do it. Mary Jane Floy/es.sister to the last witness said" Will" came to see her on Friday night. Soon after he had departed he returned and she saw his face bleediee. He told her Turner had done itand she went with him to the In firma ry. Thomas Donoghue, brother of the cemplainant,said he a.ccomnaeied him to the Police Court on Saturday morn- ing. He repel red tne conversation which took place in Mr. Hunt's offiee. Mr. A. Browne, for ttek defence, said they kad got to try a most extraordinary case, which was not corrobo- rated as to the actual assault. The complainant said he was perfectly sober, and also said the two constables were sober. He .further stated that no one was about. He (Mr. Browne) did not believe their worships would beliere that statemont when they considered that it occurred in Winwick-st., one of the principal streets in the tows, and at such an early hour of the night. Con- stable Turner denied the charge, and he was going to prove that by Constable Newsy. Both were en special duty in plain clothe., and they told him it was a quar- ter to eleven when they got into Winwick-st. They Were ! standing near Mr. Price's lodging house when they saw a young man step a man and woman. They then heard the young man (who afterwards was found to be the complabienr) call the mem-in some foul namel, and the man bit Donoghue. Turner went across the street, Newey remaining on the footpath, and the man and woman went towards the Central Station. On cooing Turner Donoghue remarked, " Are you his b-mate P" Turner replied, "No," and on Newsy coming up Donog- hue siid,"You hit me on the nose." Newey denied doing so and Donoghue then accused Turner. Mr. Browne referred to Turner's good character, and said if they convicted him, it was bound to tell against him as !a Ipoliceman. P.C.Newey stated that Constable Turner was walking across the street when a man struck Drmoglme. He (witness) followed Turner and saw the complainant's nose bleeding. Donoghue then told witness that he had struek him. The reason he did not apprehend the man who struck the hlew was that he did not consider the wound as serions as what it turned out to be. They accompanied Donoghue to a house,and told him to come to the Police Station if he had a complaint to make. The magistrates retired, and after some minutes' deliheration,the chairman (Mr. John Burgess) said there was a dlference of opinion on the Bench', and the case would he dismissed.

div.head: MURDER OF A. HUSBAND AT LIVERPOOL. STRANGE REVEL XTIONS.
div.p: MURDER OF A. HUSBAND AT LIVER- POOL. STRANGE REVEL XTIONS.

A remarkab!e case came . before Mr. Justice Day at the Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday. Margaret Walker aged Bfty-three, shopkeeper, was indicted for the mur- der of her husband, John Walker, in November last. The couple had been married five years, during which time they had lived in wretchedness. Both husband and wife indulged in drink, and the woman was jealens in disposition.. Being convinced of her husband's faithless- ness, she beat him, imprisoned .him in a bedroom, and kept him in durance there for four months, having a chain and padlock on the door so that it was impossible for thE man to escape. Once his sister was allowed to see him. She found him in a dazed condition. Not long afterwards there were sounds of scuffling in the room, and cries of" Murder." The accused admitted that one day she entered the bedchamber, took the chain off the door, and struck her husband on the head with it. The man was found dead, and his body bore shocking marks of violence. His Lordship during the hearing of the case said it was hardly conceivable that in these days, in the heart of a city like Liverpool, a man could be imprisoned in such a manner. He could not understand how the matter had escaped the attantion of the police. T:10 woman was found guilty of rtsurder and was sen- tnaccd to deah, protesting meanwhile that she was iailocent.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT EARLESTOWN.

The annual meeting of the Earlestown polling district of the Newton Conservative Association was held in the Conservative Club, Eirlestown, on Monday evening. Mr. C. B. F. Blrron, C.C.,presided, supported by Messrs. Robert. Stone, J.P., W.H.Owen (Rainhill), W. Touchstone, of the National Union of Conservatives, and W. CAlingwood. There was a large attenaance. The Chairman in opening the proceedings said the past year had been of a remarkable kind, and would bear its mark in political history for a considerable time, for it must be remembered that dur- ing that time the Home Rule Bill, which was so long kept in the dark for many years maturing under the wings of Mr. Gladst6ne, was brought to light, and they had after cousiderable examination found that it was a bill which did not meet the -requirements isf the coun- try, and to their satisfaction the Lords threw it out, and it was now he hoped dead and buried. (Hear.hear.l Since that time the next event which had occurred had been the retirement of Mr. Gladstone. He had laid aside the sword of office, and he hoped he might be long spared to use the axe which he so ably handled in the forests of Hawarden for many a long day. (Hear,hear.) They could not allow the opportunity to pass without recognising the great abilities Mr. Gladstone bad shown. During a lone time he had served both his Queen and country, and they wished him during the remainder of his life, peace. and happiness. (Applause.). They had no election and no great call upon their services during the past year, but the services they had rendered during the registration had been rendered ungrudgingly, and they would know by the results that they had increased their party in that divi- sion, and they might look forward should a crisis arrive again and the country be called upon to elect a Parlia- ment, they would find this constituency to return a member who would support Conservatives and Conser- vative prineiples (Applause.) The minutes of the test annual meeting were then read and confirmed. Mr. Borron was re-elected chair- man of the district, and he said nothing would be left undone on his part to fill the past to the best of his, ability. Dr. Handyside was re-elected vice-chairman. Mr. J. H. Moserop was reappointed secretary and trea- surer. Messrs. T. Havlden, J. Jones, J. Howe, and J. Smith were re-elected delegates to the council. The whole of the committee was re-elected. Mr. R. Stone moved the following resolution " That this meeting desires to express its gratitude to Lord Salisbury, and the Unionist leaders for their untiring efforts to preserve the union of the British Empire. and also begs to thank them for the careful and just criticism made by them upon the various measures of domestic policy introduced into the House of Parlioment last session." He had read very often la Conservative papers that this had been a barren session, bathe did not think that it was altogether barren, as it showed them the value of that part of the Constitution the House of Lords. (Applause.) Mr. W. Mills eeconded,and Mr. W. Touchstone speaking in support said there were very few places in which he took a ereater interest than that district, as he remem- bered how staunchly they had stood by the Conservative cause. After alluding to the object of the gathering, he said he would call their attention to the departure of Mr Gladstone from the world of politics, he who had the good fortune to be mixed up with politicians of great power such as Sir Robert Feel, Lord Palmerston, and Earl Ruesell,and while he was associated with them and kept within reasonable, bounds, he was a fairly useful man. He never was an admirer of Mr. Gladstone, and he was not new going to creep down. (Laughter,) He had always said he was overrated and dangerous, and he repeated that night that there was no reason that they should express regret at his retirement,except that they should regret he had made such a bad finish. He then proceeded to criticise Mr. Glaistone's career, and maintained that he never had a policy. He touched upon the question of Local Veto, and the Employers' Liability bill, and after dealing at length with the Home Rule bill, the resolution was put and unanimously car- ried.
After the usual votes of thanks the meeting termin- ated.

div.head: ROWLAND HILL, THE ECCENTRIC
div.p: ROWLAND HILL, THE ECCENTRIC
PREACHER.

At Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, on Monday evening, the Rev. John Hugh Morgan, of Altrinc- ham, delivered his popular lecture on "Rowland Hill, the eccentric preacher." The chair was occupied by Mr. R. Cooke of P-mketh. The Chair- man expressed his pleasure at being present' at that meeting that night. Be had always taken a deep interest in Bewsey-road chapel, even before it was built: Be had the honoar of being among those who took the first steps from the inception of the movemeat up to the time when the building was complete. He saw the first brick which was put down. The building ef the chapel was a gnat effort at that time in Warrington. The chapel was estimated to cost £4.390, but the actual cost was £7,055. When the opening services took place, they were £l,lOO in debt, but he was glad to say that thit had all been paid raff now, and the place was free from debt. (Applause.) •Be had been secretary of the trust in the circuit for 25 years, and to show how the pro- perty had increased during that period he might say that then the property was worth £9,694. To-day it was worth £36,613,n0t including Stockton Heath chapel and Ellesmere-street mission of which the returns had not yet come in. In addition to this, there were new schools built in the circuit, se that he thought it a most gratifying state of affairs.—The liev. J. H. Morgan then proceeded with his lecture. He said that at present,eccen- trio people were much rarer than they used to be. The increase of social intercourse had caused men to grow too much like each other, and sunk much of their in- dividuality. In many cases, 'eccentricity was merely the outward manifestation of genius, and this applied to Rowland Hill who with all his singularities combined a moral fortitude. He was born in Hawkeibury, Salop,on August 23, 1754, and he was remarkable for his liveli- ness of manner and redundancy of spirits from a very early life. He went to Cambridge, where he was the open champion of earnest Christianitvl and he became the target of violent reproach and raillery on this ac- count. After his college days,he was appointed to Surrey Chapel, London, to which place he remained true to his deatlf. He was a great open air preacher, and at times preached to 20,000 people. He died in 1833 in tho 89th year of his age. During his life he preached 23,003 ser- mons, and was a most acceptable preacher, moving his congregation to laughter and tears with equal facilitr. His noble presence contributed greatly to his power as a preacher. The lecturer during the course of the lecture gave a large Munber of amusing aneedotes and other in- cidents in the life of'llowland Hill, which he did in the true Welsh style, and they were theroughly appreciated by the audience.—The Rev. Owen Watkins announced at the close of the lecture that the collections taken at the anniversary amounted to £2B 17s. 60.-A vote of thanks to the lecturer and chairman, proposed by the Rev. J. Kirtlan, seconded by Mr. E. Place, brought the meeting to a close.

LETAL CROSSING ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN.

On Saturday mQrning shortly after eight o'clock, an accident happened at the level crossing below Fairclough-st., which connects Niessrs. Evans and Co.'s private line with the L. & N.W.R. Co.'s main line,resulting in a horse belonging to Mr. P. Thomp- son, grocer, being killed. It appears the horse and van, the latter loaded with loaves of bread, was be- ing driven in the direction of Wargrave, by a lad, and when nearing the crossing he was ordered to stop by Messrs. Evan's man, as a train of waggons were being propelled by one of the L. & N.W. Co.'s engines, from their line to Messrs. Evans. Immedi- ately after the lad was told to get over the crossing but when passing over the horse fell across the rails, before it could be removed, the leading wagon of the train passed over its legs nod the next wagon over its body, cutting it in two, and causing the wagon to leave the metals. The horse was then pushed several 3 ards along the rails,before the train could be stopped. The van was also damaged, and the brakesman, who was on the leading wagon, saved himself by jumping.

div.head: HATDOCK CILICIERT AND BOWLING CLUB.
div.p: HATDOCK CILICIERT AND BOWLING CLUB.

The first part of the programme consisted of vocal and instrumental selections kindly arranged by Mr. W. S. Barrett, consisting of a pianoforte solo, "Arabesque," by Miss C. Barrett, song, "Biddy Aroo," Mr. 3. C. Barrett, song„"Off to Phila- delphia," Mr. J. C. Barrett, duet, " %%There are you going to my pretty maid 24 Miss and Mr.H. Barrett. div.head: CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. NEWTON.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. NEWTON.

In connection with the Young People's Society of Christian Endeavour,a service of song entitled" The Prodigal Son."was given in the schoolroom on Tue.,- day evening by members of the society. There was a large audience, who thoroughly enjoyed the ser- vice, which was very cleverly rendered. Miss M. Birks gave the connective readings, on 4 besides the choir, the following submitted solos in an efficient manner, Misses E. Jones, G. Rothwell, L. Randall, A. Carlton, F. Roberts, and l. Urquhart. Miss H. Pennington gave a violin solo,and Misses K. Hughes P. Thompson and S. E. Tasker in turn accompanied on the piano. During an interval, the President of the society, the Rev. James Allatt, stated that the collection which would then be :token, would be devoted to a fund for sending delegates to the Lon- don convention, which would be held during Whit week. Since its formation the Society had made very substantial progress, and when formed was the firs*, in the Warrington district, The total num- ber of societies now in active work in this country was upwards of 1200, and the amount of useful work which they accomplished, forming as they did a connecting link between the school and church was indeed gratifying. OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIETY.

The usual weekly P.S. meeting in Wycliffe Church, was held on Sunday aftertioonond vras largely atte:.ded. Mr. Thompson, Sankey Bridges, presided, and delivered a short address on the molt ) 4 the P.S.A. Society. The Rev. W.J.Kirkland, of Warring,ton, deivered theaddress for the afternoon, his subject being " Jerry Building." He referred to the tactics of unscrupulous builders who had earned for themselves the name of j-Try and said he was very glad nit the powers that be had invested their corporations and local authori ies with some measure of authority to keep these men in check. But with all their checks somehow or other this k;nd property got run up. He brought before his he trers the importance of choosing good materials wherewith to build a good character, remarking that every charae-ter was the prAuct of choice and selection. "Tae I:3,ter Land " was sung as a solo by Niiss Seton in her usual excellent manner. Mr. R. H. PeArson presided at the organ. The Rev. J. Yonge, Messrs. J. Irish and W. Lowe, also twill p trt in the meeting.

div.head: ENCE.
div.p: ENCE.

At the Wesleyan chapel Earlestown, on Sunday evening last, the Rev. T. Wynn-Jones, in the course of his sermon made some reference to the loss sus- tained by the body in the death of 'Mr. John Pres- cott. His text was chosen from the 13 chap. All's, 36 and 37 verses. After alluding to the fact that public characters were public possession, he said John Prescott was an exemplary citizen. He, the preacher, had during two and a half years he had been there, had many opportunities of getting to know him, and he would venture to say that Mr. Prescott believed that the environments of the , workingman could never be too happy and bright. I He had a grand ideal for the workingman. He believed that cleanliness was next to godliness. John Prescott ascended the pnlit of the Methodist Church, because he firmly believed that God meant I him to ascend it. Some of his hearers perhaps thought he was a little narrow in some things, but be stuck to old fashioned theology. They might say that his culture was not broad enough to take in modern phrases of thought, but his culture was deep enough to go down to the foundation of Chris- tian faith, and strong enough to soar up an the wings of faith and reach the highest goal of the Christian belief. What it lacked in broadness it achieved in height and love. If he could get his conscience in a direct line with the express will of God, there was no power that could keep him away from that end. God said to him, Go, serve, suffer, and save, and be obeyed.

div.head: No. 1 CONVENTION OF COOD TEMPLARS.
div.p: No. 1 CONVENTION OF COOD TEMPLARS.

The monthly session of No.l Convention of South West Lancashire, was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon. The meeting was called to order at 3-30. Bro. a Clarke C.0.T., presided and there was a large attendance of repre- sentatives and deputies from various lodges in the area of the division. After the appointment of the Press and Credential Committees, the reports of the officers were received. The C.T. Bro. Clarke and the secretary, Bro. E. Newman, gave interesting accounts of the lodges. Showing them to he doing active work, and favourably organised. Bro. A. Morris, C.S.J.T., gave an encouraging report of the juvenile temple. Bro. Lindon, G.C.S., referred to the electoral matters, and concluded by moving the .following resolution, which was seconded by Bro. A. Francis, and adopted, viz.. "That this Conven'- tion representing lodges in Warrington, Widnes,St. Helens, Earlestown. Ashton, Hindley, thee, Wigan and Leigh respectfully requests the cabinet to. reintroduce early next session the Liquor Traffic (Local Control) Bill, and further urges the Govern- ment to use every legitimate means to pass this righteous and expedient measure through all its stages, during the coming session of Parliament." The question of extending the order by the institu- tion of new lodges and temples carte up,and was dis- cussed at length, and eventually a committee was appointed to consider and further the object. The next place of meeting was fixed for Widnes, when a paper is to he read by Bro. Newman, CA. A paper was afterwards read by Bro. E. Middleton, C.C., of Leigh, entitled "Alcohol, its physical and moral effects." The paper was of an educational character, and proved interesting .to all. The thanks of the Convention were tendered the escayist, and also to the Earlestovvn friends for their , arrangements, and the session concluded shortly after six o'clock. A public tea followed to which a large number sat down, and at the close ,a meeting was held presided over by Mr. G. Dring. of Earlea- town, when addresses were given by Bros. Long- worth, D.S.J.T.. Manchester, 'Roberts (Warrington . Lindon (Prescot), and the Chairman, interspersed ! with vocal and instrumental music. A resolution es fellow, moved by Bro. J. Taylor and seconded by Bro. Lindon was unanimously adopted, "That 1 this meeting respectfully urges the Government to reintroduce the Liquor Traffic (Local Cortrol) Bill ' into l'arliament early next seasion,and to use every legitimate means to pass it into law with the least possible delay."

THE House of Commons has this A SVignificant week passed a resolution declaring ote. that the p owers now exercised by the hereditary legislators of the House of Lords should cease. It would nct be easy to over-rate the significance of that event. Of course, much is being said to belittle it and to make it appear as of no importance. We are told that it was a "snatch-vote," that the resolution was only car- ried by a majority of two in a comparatively thin that the majority was composed entirely of Radicals and Irishmen, and that even the Government would not accept the mandate con- tained in the resolution. But after all this has been said, the salient fact remains that the House of Commons—the popularly elected Chamber—has in the usual and constitutional way declared that the time has now come when the Peers shall be divested of the privileges which they abuse by mutilating and destroying progrePsive legislation. That is a fact which there is no getting beyond. It testifies with unmistakable clearness to the . great advance which has been made this last year or two with the question of the reform of the loose of Lords. Hitherto most of the pronounce - nents on the subject have partaken largely of the nature of" pious opinions," but a great change has been wrought by the vote of Tuesday evening. A reform for which the House of Commons has cast a majority comes at once within the region of practical politics. Ministers and political leaders generally have naturally hesitated before plung- ing into an enterprise of such great pith and mo- ment as that of the abolition or re-construction of . the House of Lords, but now Mr. LABOUCHERE ' and those wh o followed him into the division lobby can fairly claim that they have broken the ice, even though they have done it in an irregular and somewhat embarrassing fashion. It is now more than ever certain that the cry for" mending or ending" the so-called Upper House will be very prominent at the next general election. As to the time when that election may 'le ex- pected there is just now, as might be expected, a very abundant crop of prophecies. The Tories and their allies profess to be anxious that it should take place at a very early period, and there • have even been some veiled threats of an attempt to force a dissolution. But Lord ROSEBERY has made it clear, just as Mr. GLADSTONE did before him, that the Government reserve to themselves the right of deciding when Parliament shall be elissolved. That is a right which they will not allow either the permanent Tory majority of Peers or the obstructive minority in the House of Com- mons to usurp. In the Meantime, as the now Premier said at the meeting of the Liberal party on Monday, there is no change in measures. The Government are as determined now as they ever were to press forward with some further large in- stalments of the Neweast,ie programme. The Queen's speech promises that there will be laid before Parliament in the session which has just opened Bills dealing with registration and the abolition Of plural voting, with disestahlishment in.
