SOME people are strongly opposed The Relief of the Poor. to what we may call the liberalis- ing of Boards of Guardians on the ground that guardians elect3d on the " one marl one vote" franchise will dispense poor-law relief with a free hand. It is a settled axiom in the minds of these people that harsh and unsympathetic treat- ment of the pauper means a saving to the rate- payer. With guardia-s who happen to be of this turn of mind out-door relief is severely discoun- tenanced, and "the house" is freely offered to the needy applicant. It is taken for panted that in-door relief is much more economical than out- door. If, however, there, be anything in an elabor- ate and apparently a closely reasoned paper contri- buted' to the " Contemporary " review by Dr. HUNTER, M.P., this is a mistake. Dr. HUNTER. makes comparisons between Unions which respectively favour the in-door and the out-door methods of relief, and he comes very decidedly to the conclusion that the ott-door system is to be recommended on the ground of economy as well as on that of being de- cidedly the more humane of the two. In London, for instance, he finds that the cost of pauperism per head of the population in the Unions which give more than an average of out-doer relief is ten shillings and sixpence; in the Unions which favour the in-door policy it is a littlo over thirteen the out-door Unions being less costly than the in-door Unions by some £300,000 a year. It appears that, next to London, Lancashire has the lowest average of out-door relief , but, according to Dr. HUNTER, the same general results are to be found here. In the in-door Unions the average cost of pauper- ism per head of the population is five shillings ; in those in which out-door relief is more freely given it is only three shillings and threepence. The same general conclusion is enforced when the whole of England and Wales is taken into account. In the in-door unions the cost is seven shillings and sevenpence, and in the out- de or five shillings and twopence. Dr. HUNTER can, if his paper stand the brunt of criticism which it will undoubtedly be subjected to, claim that he has done a very im- portant public service. On the score of considera- tion for the poor there is no question that the out- door administration of relief is preferable to the workhouse. If it turn out to be cheaper as well, here i s not much left to be said for "the house."

Mr. W. T. STEAD has been spend- The Great ing a few months in Chicago and Republic. the opinions he has formed of the Americans are somewhat mixed. In municipal government at all events the Old Country has got nothing to learn from the Great Republic of the West. T'Aere are, Mr. STEAD tells us, sixty-eight aldermen in the City Council of Chicago, and of these fifty are admittedly corrupt. They aro aldermen that they may make money by trading with speculators. Saloon-keepers and gamblers "boss' the municipal government of the city, and , as for the administration of justice it would, says Mr. STEAD in his uncompromising way, be regarded as disgraceful in the worst parts of Russia and bring a blush to the cheek of a pacha. Drunkenness and politics seem to be regarded as the two most demoralising vices in what we are proudly told by our transatlantic cousins is the land of the free. If a man wants to be converted to republican principles he should, it seems, keep away from America. Mr. STEAD thiuks that Russia and the United States are very much alike in many respects, and especially in the jealous safeguards which the constitution of each provides to prevent the people from having their own way or being permitted to decide their own destinies. The " Dead Hand " of old constitution makers paralyses progress in the States, and, in particular, the rigid constitutional machinery is brought into operation to thwart the efforts of the working classes to improve the conditions under which they live. There is, however, not a little to 'be said on the other side. It is hardly fair to compare a country in which such a man as Mr. Hopkins, the Mayor of Chicago, can come to the top with the stagnant and stereotyped empire of the Czars. Twenty years ago Mr. Hopkins was a "lumber shover" in the Pulnaan timber yards. Now he is the leading citizen of the second city of America and fighting heroically for honesty ad good government against all the forces of vice and demoralisition.

STRANG'S Want ON A WIDNES WOMAN. A married woman namen Emily Sarah Jervis, aged 23, of Mill-road, died under painful circumstances. several weeks ago she saved a child from being run over at great risk to herself. This, owing to her condi- tion, gave her a great shock. A few days afterwards she was se:zed with cramp whilst going downstairs, but she did not seem to be injured. On Saturday night she went to bed, And was unable to get up again and died en Wednesday morning. The Coroner has been com- municated with, but he does not think an inquest neces- sary.

HALTON ROAD BMA; CLASS, RIINCORS. Under the auspices of this class on Monday evening a lecture was given in Mill Brow School by Mr. Frith on "llluminatin and other gases." The chair was occu- pied by the conductor of the class, the Rev. W. Arrow- smith. The lecturer dealt with his subject in a very interesting meaner by means of diagrams, and illustrated it by. a number of brilliant experiments showing the Properties of various gases as well as the properties and structure of flame and illuminosity. The safety and dangers of coal gas as an illuminating agent compared with others were fully and amply enumerated and ex- plained. Mr. S. M. Tenaporly proposed, and Mr. Pope seconded, a hearty vote of thanks to the lecturer which was unanimously accorded.

The Runcorn Tonic-Sol Fa Prize Choir are happy in the possession of a conductor whose only object, it is to watch over their welfare. Mr. Holford has now been their con luctor for nine years during which time he has worked very hard to bring the members up to the high standard of efficiency which they at present occupy. At their social gathering the other evening they suitably recog- nised the meritorious work which their conductor had discharged in the course of his long connection with them by presenting him with a handsome writing desk. From the expressions of Mr. 11w.Thes on behalf of the, choir and.those of Mr. Holford it mug surely be a pleasure for the members to work under such a master and equally pleasurable for the master to conduct such pupils.

The condition of trade in Runcorn had been any- thing but flourishing in the course of the past few months. This is largely due perhaps to the com- pletion of the Ship Canal and the fact that a large number who were employed there, and who had come from other parts, have remained it,.re to swell the multitude of unemployed. There is fortunately every appearance at present that better times are in store for Runcorn as preparations are actively in progress at the Sprinch for the erection of several large barges for t.he use of the Ship Canal Company. It is to be hoped that the further developements proposed in connection with the Runcorn section of the Canal, and which are so anxiously looked for- ward to by the working classes, will soon commence.

Fortunately, some of the reports of the recent accident on the Ship Canal at Runcorn are incor- rect. Of course, the accident as it is takes a most serious form, but it would have been a matter for deeper regret had the barge sunk in the Canal which would thus have had the obvious effect of creating a block of traffic along the waterway. Such, however, was not the case, es the vessel was successfully placed upon a mud bank where. the necessary repairs will be made.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
MONTHLY MEETING.

The members of this body held their usual monthly meeting on Wednesday afternoon at the offices, the cemetery. There were present Mr. T. Handley (in . the chair), the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. H. Colburn, T. Whittaker, R. Morris, and Wm. Salkeld I:secretary). - The financial statement was submitted sad showed that the interments for the eleven months ending February 25th numbered 481, as against 429 in the corresponding period of last year. During that time fees had beer received amountiag to £451 is. 2d. compared with £4lO Bs. 24. last year.—The Finance Committee's minutes contained a recommenda- tion to pay accounts to the amount of £5l ss. 81., in addition to the cheque due for interest to the extent of £slloa. 10d.—The Secretary produced a letter from Mr. Michael Barker, surveyor, stating that the Com- missioners contemplated rounding off the corner of Norman-road and Greenway-road if arrangements could be made with the Burial Board and the trustees of the Bethesda Manse. A plan was enclosed showing'the piece of land required, which ineacired abont eighteen yards. The improvement would nessit- ate the removal of some small building in the corner and perhaps the dispensing with the doors in the wall which he thought were not now used. Perhaps the Board would say if the improvement could be brought about, and upon what conditions.—Mr. Handley thought that th 3 improvement would be a good one. The London and North Western Railway Company had effected a similar curve on the opposite side to the one proposed, and the appearance was very good.—The secretary said that the shed was provided for the dressing of head stones, Stc. These were now to a great extent dressed at the works of private firms so that the building was not now re• quired as mnch as formerly.—The other members pre- sent expressed the opinion that the carrying out of the proposal would prove beneficial.—The Chairman, in re- ply to Mr. Coleman, said he thought it was not necessary to consult the ratepayers on the subj4ct : They were not co,nplying with the wish of a private individual, but a public authority.—Finally the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi moved and Mr. Morris seconded that the wish of the Commis- sioners be complied with, providing that the shed is re-erected, the doors replaced, that the work be performed to the satisf oction of the Board, and that the position of the Board should be as good when the work was completed as at the present time.— rho usual notices for the appointment of two auditors of the Board's accounts for the year ending March 25th were signed, likewise one to the overseers to pay the half-yearly call of £6O for the sinking fund in June next.—The Secretary intimated to the members that the very severe storms experienced during the past winter lad seriously affected the cemetery lodge and the Dissentrb' chapel ,and particularly the wnedn spire. It was not well fastened, was in an exposeil position, and the gases from the alkali works had a detritnental effect open the iron work. A considerable quantity of lead had been required to keep rain off, which was doing con- sideraisle damage out of the chapel. He had considered it advisable to get the work done as senn_as possible. He was afraid that on one occasion the work had inter- fered with Dr. Gastaldi whiLit lie was officiatiug at a

funeral, and if so he was exceedingly sorry. He asked the Board to approve of the proceedings he had taken and sanction the payment of the costs incurred by the repairs.—The chairman considered it a pity that a stone tower was not provided for the Nonconformist chapel like the one connected with the building used by the Church people. Was the one composed of stone to show the superiority of churchneople over their Nonconformist brethren ?—The Board confirmed the action of the secre- tary.

SOCIAL GATHERING AT RUNCORN. THE TONIC SOL FA CHOIR AND ITS CONDUCTOR. A most enjoyable social gathering wider the auspices ot the Runcorn Tonic Sol Fa Prize Choir took place on Monday evening in the Ellesmere- street schoolroom. About 130 choristers and friends partook of an excellent tea which was served by the following ladies, assisted by several gentlemen members of the choir :—Mrs.Newall, Mrs. J. Stubbs, Miss Massey and Miss Withington. After tea pre- parations were made for a convivial evening, Mr. Hugh Hughes presiding. Mr. Holford, who has been conductor of the choir since its formation nine years ago, was present, and addressed the members at some length. This was the first time he had met them together since their perform- ance of " Jephtlia," and he wished to seize the oppor- tunity for the purpose ?f congratulating them upon their appearance and singing. Lie had no hesitation in saying that never had they either looked or sang better than on that occasion and it must have been highly gratifying to them, as well as to himself, to hear the unanimous praises of those who formed the audience. He hoped, however, that they would guard against the idea that now they had attaiLed such success that they could rest on their oars for a while. If they did, their powers would deteriorate. It was the duty of every individual member to attain the highest possible degree of efficiency, in order that the general effect might be improved. (Applause.) This concluded their ninth season as a Choral Society. When they started, they seemed to have very little in their favour except the love of music and the capacity for hard work and it was only those who joined the choir at its formation who knew the hard fortunes with which they were beset. Ha was glad, however, to see that their work was now appreciated, and that now the " flowing tide" was with them. Let them do their utmost to deserve the public support,and he was sure it would be forthcoming. They -should look upon the society as their own, and endeavour to the utmost ex- tent of their powers to improve it. (Applause.) He thanked them for attendance at rehearsals which had indeed been most successful, notwithstanding the incon- veniences they had been put to. In conclusion, he ex- pressed a hope that they would be soared many more successful seasons. (Applause.) Mr. Hughes then briefly addressed the members, and in the course of his remarks referred to the many and valuable services which had been discharged by Mr. Holford for the good of the choir. It had been an up- hill fight for them, but he was sure that it had been doubly so for Mr.Holforcl. He had, therefore,the great- est pleasure in asking him to kindly aceept a small pre- sent as a token of esteem fro:n the meinh..rs of the choir. (Applause.) Mr. Hughes then handed to Mr. Holford the key or a handsome writing, desk which had been purchased by private subscriptions from the choir. Mr. Holford, who was deeply moved by this appar- ently unexpected turn of affairs, said be did not antici- pate anything of this nature taking place. He might assure them that the work he had done in the past,purely sprung from a desire for the welfare of the choir without any idea of a reward of this kind. Of course it was very gratifying to know that his efforts had been so appre- eiared, and he was very thankful to them for this ex- pression of their appreciation. (Applause.) The remainder of the evening was spent by the mem- bers in a spirit of conviviality.

Alderman Wareing said he was glad to see the Mayor amongst them again and hoped that he had benefited by his holiday.—The Mayor suitably replied.
HIGHWAY COMMITIHE.

This Committee reperted that the Town Clerk had had an interview with Capt. Clanchy, R.N., and that that gentleman had promised to take the necessary steps for the protection of the public in West Bank-st. by the erection at an early date of properly locked gates in con- nection with the level crossings belonging to the Hutch- inson estate, and that in the meantime a watchman should he regularly employed to warn the public of the danger by passing trains; but that he (Capt. Clanchy) could not accept any responsibility with respect to per- sons passing over the West Bank Dock sidings to and Iron the works upon the Marsh, as he contended that the public had no right of way over the sidings in question. —Resolved tint the Borough Surveyors be and is hereby directed to see that the proposeci work 4 in West Bank-street are duly carried out.—Building plans: The following plans were submitted by tho Surveyor :—New Post Office Buildings, Victoria Square, disapproved; Circus, Ditton-road, disapproved; Primi- tive Methodist School, Waterloo-road, disapproved; Hotel, Albert-road, approved; six cottages, Walter-st., approved; two cottages, Bradshaw-st., approved.—The confirmation of the minutes was msved by Councillor Quinn and seconded by Councillor Christie.—Councillor Gough said he was very glad to see that they were to have gates placed at the level crossing in West Bank-st. —Councillor Smith stated that the back passa,ge in the rear of Mersey-road was in a dangerous condition and injurious to health and wished to know when the High- way COmmittee would be able to take up the making of back pas2ages.—Councillor Quinn in replying said the reason why the back passage at the rear of Mersey-road had not been made, was because they had not yet ap- plied to the Local Government Board for the money but it would be sent in with the nelt batch.—The minutes were passed.

IIEALTII COMMITTEE. A meeting of this Committee was held an the 2nd March. The Town Clerk submitted notice from the Board of Agriculture, declaring Widnes to be part of an area infected with swine fever, for the purposes of the Swine Fever (Infected Areas) Order of 1894. Resolved that Supt. Keighley and Inspector Pattison, Inspectors under the said Acts, and Police Sergeants Charles McGregor, Robert Strickland, James Ratcliffe, George Carter and Walter Bennett be, and they are hereby authorised, to grant licenses on Lobalf of the local authority of this Borough for the movement ot swine in accordance with the said Orders. Resolved that Mr. A. Shawcross, M.R.C.V.S., be appointed Veterinary Inspec- tor for the Borough. Hospital reports; Ateident hospi- tal, number of patients at last meeting, 5 ; admitted since, 8 ; discharged, 3 ; died, 0 ; patients still in, 8. The cases of Infectious Diseases notified were as follows : Enteric fever, 3 ; erysipelas, 5 ; membratiou s croup, 7 ; scarlet fever, 3 ; total; 18. It was satisfactory to note that the dean rate has diminished considerably-132 per 1,000 against 21.2 per 1.000 last month.—Councillor Hodgkinson proposed the adopticu of the minutes.— Councillor O'Donnell spoke as to justice not being done to the tradespeople in the distribution of orders for goods.—Councillor Hocigkinson said that this matter would receive attention ia future.—The minutes were passed.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. A special meeting was held on the 20th Feb. The report of the gas and water engineer with reference to the fire in Mersey-road, on the 14 February, having been read, the Committee proceeded to inveatiz- ate the circumstances connected with the fire, and heard the statements of the members of the brigade and others present upon the occasion with reference thereto. Resolved that the further consideration of the matter, be adjourned to the 27th Feb.when a meeting was held,and it was resolved that the report of the gas and water engineer be not accepted. The monthly meeting was held on! the 6th inst. Gas tests: The report of tests made on the 15th and 23rd inst. read as follows : Illum- inating power 1618 and 18.47 candles respectively. The mean rainfall for the month had he 2150 inches. Water delivered in February 82,344,669 gallons. a gainst 69,435,215 gallons in the correvonding month of last year. Gas delivered 16,571,000 cubic feet, agetin.st 14,424,000 cubic feet in the corresponding month of last year.—Rectric bells for fire station : Resolved, that the engineer obtain amended tenders for the supply and fix- ing of electric alarm . crimmunications in accordance with the arrangements approved by the Committee.— Alderman Tim mis proposed adoption of minutes.—Coun- cigar Singleton wished to know the result of the recent investigation in regard.to the fire brigide.—Aldertnan Timmis said the evidence and report would be put on the table for confidential perusal.—Minutes pas;ed. GENERAL PIIRPOSEA AND PARLIAMENTARY comet term At a meeting held on the 7th inst. it was resolved that the Town Clerk convene a meeting of the aldermen at en early date, with reference to the alderman'c robes.— Aldermen Wareing proposed and Councillor Shores seconded the adoption of the minutes.—CounciUor Barlow referred to the aldermanic robe: and maid they had not yet had the pleasure of seeing the aldermen in 1 their robes.—Alderman Wareing said that the matter Ihad been held over through the Mayor's-absenee, but probably at the next meeting of the Council, Councillor Barlow's desires would be fulfilled .—Minutes passed.

The report of the Snecial Committee appointed to con- sider the question of providing a public cemetery for the Borough was submitted. This Committee reported that they had visited the various burial grounds and were of the opinion that the provision of a further place or places for the interment of the dead wag necessary, aed they thought it expedient that a public general cemetery should be provided and maintained by the Corporation. —Councillor Christie proposed that the question be ad- journed for 12 montlis.—Councillor Wright seconded,and said he thought the Committee had rushed through the matter. They should have given particulars as to land required and the cut.—Six voted in favour of the mat- ter being adjourned for 12 mouths and 12 against. The report was, therefore, adepted.—C.)uncillor Hodgkinson moved and Alderman Williamson seconded " That the repert of the Special Committee appointed on the 9th of May, 1893, to report as to the necessity for providing a. Cemetery for the Borough, and adopted by the Council at their present meeting, he referred to the Parliamen- tary and General Purposes Committee, and that they be instructed to select and submit to the Council one or more sum able site or sites, together with an estimate of the cost of the same and ot providing and maintaining thereon a Cemetery necessary for the present and future r. quirements of the Borough and to report as te the beet and most appropriate method of establiihing such Cemetery."—The motion Pitt 3 adopted.

div.head: lIEETING OF PRESBYTERIANS AT
div.p: lIEETING OF PRESBYTERIANS AT
RUNCORN.
A YEAR'S WORK.

On Thursday evening the annual meeting in con- nection with the St. John's Church, Runcorn, was held. The chair was occupied by the Pastor, the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, and the attendance was large, the Rev. R. G.. Jones and Mr. Laidlaw, both of Liverpool, being present as a deputation from the Presbytery. The Rev. Pulford Williams presented his report which Stated that the accounts of the past year re-aected very commendably upon the faithfulness and generosity of those connected with St. John's Church. The year of 1333 had been, in many respects a trying ' one, great depression had been felt in trade, several of I the most useful members had left the town, and some of them had had to pass through the crucible of suffering. INotwithstanding they had felt in a marked degree the I presence of Him who had said " Lo, I am with you always." From many points of view it had been a pros- perous as well as a notable year. The Sunday school had attained this year to an unprecedented average,and their recently inaugurated Y.P.S.C.E. had already given an instance of its sinszular power in d',.epening the spiritual life of the church. This year they would be required to leave the premises in which they now i,y6r.mipped. The new building was already ; up its arms towards Heaven. They would carry with them many tender memories associated with the old chapel. According to the financial statement the bAl,nee at thp c,mmeneement of the year wa. £8 3s. Bd. the rocvipts doring the year amounted to £235 is. 2d.; expen.e. £222 19 thus leaving a balance in hand of £2O ss.—The pastor said the membership during the past three }ears had doubled, and the work in connec- tion with the new school was satisfactorily progressing; Iso much so that there was every possibility of it being ready for possession about Whitsuntide.—The Rev. R. 6. Jones and Mr. Laidlaw congratulated the members and officials upon the important and successful work whici was being carried on and encourged them to con- tinue in their earnest efforts to further the cause of the Master in the district.

div.p: FRODSIIIM.

LECTURE ON "CHRIST AND CIIINA."—Or. Moniay evert- ing the W. J. ‘Vilkitii (ftisistant secretary of the Reli- gious Tract Society) delivered a lecture en •4 Christ and China," in the Town hail, Frodsham. There was a tairly large audience,a.nd the chair was occupied by the Rev. A. r. Reynol4s, vicar of Kingslay. The Lecturer spoke of the peculiarities of this race of peonle (Chinese) and their various methods of worship. lie illustrated his suhject with dissolving views,a.nd mad: it extremely interesting to all. The lecture was delivered under the auspices of the Missionary Work and Religious Tract Societyeand at the termination of the proceedings a col- lection was made co its behalf amounting to £3 185.91 d. This sum is in addition to the subscriptions which have been received in aid cf the missionary work of tne so- ciety.

div.head: BELSBY.
div.p: BELSBY.

CONCERT IN THE WESLEYAN SUNDAY Scoots.—With the object nf augmenting the funds of this school the members of the Mersey Drum and Fife Band, Runcorn, gave a miscellaneous entertainment on Monday evening in the schoolroom. There was a crowded attendance and the proceedings were presided over by Mr. William Shaw, missionary, who spoke in terms of praise of the spiritual work which was being carried on at the school. The programme was admirably arra ngol and was opened by the band who contributed the " White Squall " in excellent style, and also" the Fisher Boy," (song and chorus). Miss Dougla3 evoked loud applause in her rendition " Dada wouldn't buy me a bow-wow," as also did Master F. Allen in his contribution " Grace Darling." The recitation "Warriors of the sea" was given in a praiseworthy manner by Mr. James Owen and Miss Bandies was heard to alvantage in the song "Angels ever bright and fair," which was duly appre— ciated. Mr. A. Penney's interpretation of "That little chair" was excellent, and Master W. Marsh's rendering - of " When you and I were yopng. Maggie" was effec- tive. The song" Every bullet has its billet" was well rendered by Mr. J. Moores and the same might be said of Master T. Shallcross who contributed " Wait till the ship Comes home." The band was again heard to advantage in their execution of " Bseford," and also a song and chorus entitled " Weighing the Anchor." Miss Douglas sang 'Gypsy Jane" in a most pleasing man- ner, and Master F. Allen did justice to his second con- tribution "Polly Wolly Noodle," which caused consider- able merriment. The Lancashire reading entitled" All meet in a grave," by Mr. Byfield, properly tickled the audience and the reader was loudly applauded. "Ora Pro Nobis " was capitally sung by Miss Randles, and Mr. A. Penny is deserving of praise for his rendering of "When other lips." The remaining items were likewise- given in an appreciative manner and consisted of songs by Mr. Moores and Mr. John Shaw, and a recitation by Mr. Jahn. The entertainment concluded with a laugh.- able farce entitled "Apartments to Let," in which ' Messrs. Wakefield, John Owen, James Owen and CM appeared as characters. Misses Nellie Waterworth and Minnie Bowyer accompanied the various singers in a \ skilful manner. At the close of the proceedings the artistes were entertained to supper by Mrs. Lowe, when votes of thanks were accorded them and also to Mr. Byfield who had defrayed the expenses incurred by the party in travelling th,ther.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
A LOCAL CASE SEITLED.
The clse of Messrs. Faircloug,h v. the Manchester Ship Canal came before Mr. Justice Kettewich yesterday in the Chancery division. -Counsel informed his lordship

that the miter had been discussed with counsel, terms arranged, and minutes signed, and asked that it might come before the court on Wednesday next. His lordship granted the application. • VISIT OF A MISSIONARY STEAMER TO RUNCORN.

'rhe new missionary seamer "John William 3," which has been built for the Lond3a M,saionary Society, was expected to dock at Ranorn last night (Friday) so as to lie on view to-day. T.be vessel is under the charge of Captain Turpie and will

remain at Runcorn until Monday, when she will proceed to Liverpool where she will be viewed during her stay at Canning Dry Doelc. and St. George's dock. This steamer has cost £17,030 and is fitted up so as to meet the most modern requirements. A further contributiort of £lO towards this sum has b-en forwarthd by the treasurer of the Runcorn AuKiliary, Mr. if:•11. Clad- wick, during the past fortnight. COLLISION NEIR RUNCORN.

An accident, which might have been attended with more serious consequences, occured on Wednesday morning at the Ship eanal,near Randtes sluices,between Runcorn and Mo-Te. It appears that the Norwegian barque " Ebenezer." laden with logwood was being towed, by the tug St. Winifred, op the canal when the gearing gear at the tog suddenly lailed and she remained motionless. The reitilt was th-it, the Ehenenr ran into the St. Winifred, and the anchlr fluke of the former was , driven into her pert bow. She began rapidly to fill with water, but fortunately the lay-by known as the stone Hdelph at Haystack was close within reach and the sink- ing vessel was successfully placed upon it, thus re- moving all danger of sinking in the -waterway. A diver was subsequently engaged and was occupied irk repairing the vessel on Wednesday. night and •chuNday - with the result that on the night of the last-named dar the vessel was again albat. There still remained, how- ever, about eleven feet of watir in her, tr.i!: plmning operations were continued-on Friday and it is expected thst she will s'aortly be able to resume her j 4urri,v te) mvielle:ter. There was no interference with on tite canal.

ALDBILIIAN HARRISON'S COB. Edward Massey. butcher, Horeemarket;st.' Was sharged with furiously driving a horse and cart to the danger of passengers at Market Gate on March Ist. P.C. Corceran who preyed the case said that the defend- ant was driving at about ten miles an hoer, and a 'bus which v, as coming along Sankey-st. had to pull up pretty leuickly :o keep out of his way.—The defendant said that his lane was a cob, 14 years of sine, and it could sot co at the rate mentioned by the officer.—Alderman Ilarrison : "Nonsense, I have a cob 18 yeare of age, and it would ,t-zo twelve miles an hour." (Laughter.)—Delandant was fined 10s. and Costs. CRUELTY TO EIORSILS. Peter Baguley, 'bus driver, Latchford, was charged at the:Warrington Borough Court yesterday, with working his horse while in an unfit state on March 7th. Inspector Luff said that he saw the defendant driving a orown horse attached to a bus coming from Sankey Bridges. Me discharged the passengersand witness then went and examined tele horse. He found it to be very lame on the forelegs, and it was sufferieg from strained tendons. —Defendant was fined 10a including costs.—William Arnold, 6ankey _Widens, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit etete en March 6th, and Samuel Baxter, green grocer, nankey Bridges,wa,s charged with sausine it to be so worked. inepectorLuff said that on March 6th lie saw Arnold in Oeford-lane. hi charge of a chestnut Deny attecl nil to a Cart laden with green gro- eery. He was hitting it to get it irno a trot. Witness netised that the horse was very lame, and was suffering born diseased feet. Arnold said that it belonged to Mr. newer, San'aef 3ridges, and said that it enae everee at sometimes than others.—P.C. Due-tale corroboraten the inspector as to the state of the horse.—The ! defendant. Baxter denied that Arnold lind a whip.—ileEwas fined Ss. and costs and Arnold was ordered to pay costs. THE TRICKSTERS CAUGHT. At the Warrington Boroueei Court on Saturday morn- lhomas Donough, 15, Iterkett-street, Liverpoonand einerge Davies, who for a short time has been livink at Percivals Fold, were charged eeith stealing by means, of a trick from John William Clare, on Thursday night is. Id. in cash, and further changed with obtaining 2d. *am Richard Morris on the same day. The evidence showed that the prisoner Donough sold to the com- plainant (lare, a youth, 19 years of age, a number of sards which he stated would, by holding to a light show a number of nice pictures and views. • He received is. lid. from Clare for them. On examining the cards, are found them to be nothing more than blank cards whigh had been purchased at Mr. Wood's Sankey-street. ' Ware went in search of the man and found him in corn- pany with two other men, the second prieoner being . one. He asked for his money back, stating that they were blank cards. The money however had been divided between the three men, and after some henta- tion a collection was made, and Donough gave Clare a shilling back. It was also shewn that the prisoner Donough sold some blank cards under the same pretence to a youth named Richard Untie. Before commencing business Donough on both oecaeiens asked the youths " Are you religious!' On Friday Clare saw the two prisoners try ing on the "same trick" with another tad in Bewsey-road, and soon afterwards meeting a police- man he informed him of the prisoners' proceedings. P.C. Woods went after theta and stopped them. They were taken into custody. arni a number of blank cards were ! found upon the prisoner Donough. The magistrates eommitted the prisoners te gee) tor 14 dare each on the nest charge, and 14 days each MI the second charge. A SLQUEL TO THE CAMPIN'S MEETING. John Mitchell, a cab driver, 22 arry-at., eves sum- moned before the Warrington magistrates on Monday on the charge of allowing his cab to stand in Witonick- at., on February 23, longer than required to take up i as- sengers.—Mr. A. Browne defended.—P.C. Delehay said Meat at 11.30 on Friday night, Feb. 23,111 Was on duty near Central Station in conapeny with P.C. Bruce, when they saw a cab opposite to Price's Temperance Hotel. There was no one with it. Inspector Luff, R.5.P.C.A.,. at that moment came up. and they kept about the same place for a quarter of an hour. Witnese then went with Inspector Luff to the hotel where there was a meeting of etabmen taking place. They went inside and were ad- mitted. into the room where the meeting was held and Mr. Jackson of Salford was speaking. They had only been inside a minute or two when Mr. Price stopped the • speaker and said that he did not know whether tne men were aware that there was a police officer and an inspec- tor for the prevention of cruelty to animals, in the rootn. He did not think that the meeting had anything to do with the police at all. Witness at d the inspector were asked to withdraw, and soon afterwards another cabman E same up. They asked him for the owner of the cab and Mitchell was brought out at about midnight. He said . *at the cab was his, and be jumped on the box and went away. Tbe cab had then 'been waiting half-an- houn—ln cross-examination witness said that he had not been ordered to go to the meeting, and thesummons was not taken out for spite.—Constable Bruen also gave evi- dence.—Mr. Browne said tbat the cab vies waiting for Mr. Jackson to take him to the railway station on the night in question, and he had been put to the inconveni- ence of walkingeowing to the cab being sent away.—The bench dismissed the case on this explanation. DEFRAUDING TIM RAILWAY COMPANY. At the Warengton Borough Court, yeeterdar, hefere -a full bench of magistrates. James Uphill, Parker-street, the local efilr.4 for the National Society for the Preven- tion of Cruelty to Children, was charged on Feb. 2nd,he unlawfully travelled on the L. and NeWellailway frome Broadheatli to Warrineton without having preferred to ' pay the fare. Mr. Fenna represented the Hallway Co., and Mr. Percy Davies defended and pleaded guilty; Mr. Fenna in opening the case said that the reason why the adjournment of the case was made on the 2nd inst. until to-day was that Mr. Davies had made to him a certain communication, which, it correct would have ottused the case to have been withdrawn. Ile (Mr. nerma) desired at the time to verify those statements, and it was his duty to say that those staterneute had net been found to be correct. They were absolutely.felse, and had aggravated the case. On February 2nd, the lefendent took a third class return ticket from Bank (nuay to Latchford. He did not alight at Latcaford,but later in the day, he was seen on the return journey at liroadheath. Same suspicion wes excited, and the nooking clerk asked for his ticket. The defendant in reply said " Dunham Massey," meaning that he was going to the'next station. There was therefore no tic- ket produced. The baoking clerk, however, was not satisfied, and the guard of the train, in which defendant went •5 !rein Broadheath was instructed to watch the defeneent -who was pointed cut to him. to .see if he get eut at Duni.am Massey. The guard accordingly watched him at Dunham Massey station, but he did not get out there, nor at any station until Bank Quay was reached. On getting out of the train at that station, he handed the return tieleet from Latchford to the collector who entered a notice to that effect in his book.—Williarn Roberts, booking clerk at Breadheath station, said that on Feb. 2riti he was on duty. The defendant alighted from the 6 57 train from Stockport, and witness asked tor his ticket to which he replied that he was going Dun- ham Massey. The train from Stockport did not go beyond Broadheeth, aud the defendant would therefore have to ctaege to go further. Witness saw .the defendant get on a train to Liverpoel. arid owing to witness's suspicions, the guard was teld to witch hiete.--Cross-examiuen : The defendant was on

Broadheath station 28 minutes. Be was sure that de- fendant mentioned Dunham Massey. His suspicions were aroused because he knew that defendant came from Warrington.—Frederick Morris, porter at Broadheath Station, and Thomas Clarke, guard of the 7.5 train from Manchester, and Wm. Holland, ticket collector at Bank Quay, gave corroborative evidence.--Mr. Fenna said r.at he applied for the costs incurred by call- ing witnesses, to be paid by the defendant. The costs would amount to 19s. 61—Mr. P. Davies, for the defence, said that the case was a most unfortunate one for the defendant, who, as the magistrates knew, held a position of trust, and often had occasion to appear in that court, in the capacity of prosecutor; an serious cases. On the seernd of February the defendant had two cases to visit, one at Latchford, and another at Wilmslow, near Stockport. He booked to Latchford. Now, the week previous defendant had caught cold at Chester Assizes and had since been suffering from a severe attack of neuralgia, which was so bad that on ' the day of the offence he did not know what he was about. It was whilst in such a state that ha neglected to leave the train at Latchford, and went on to Stock- port. The defendant had withdrawn an accusations which he had made against the Railwa' Company, and in addition, had offered to contribute £5 to their Bene- volent Fund and to make a horn tole apology. if they would refrain from taking proceedings.—Mr. Greener, secre- tary to the N.S.P.C.C., said he had known the defendant same time and had always regarded his actions as up- right and straightforward.—Alderman Harrison said they were sorry that a man in defendant's position ap- peared before them in such a case, but they would have t o fine him 203. aid costs, and to order him to pay witnesses costs.

div.head: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY'S
div.p: RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY'S
CONCERT.

The Runcorn Musical Society gave their third grand concert of the season on Wednesday evening in the Public flan, Runcorn. The programme was of a miscellaneous nature. consisting of selections from the compositions of some of the most renown- ed masters of Music. The attendance was not so largo as might have been anticipated, the body of the hall being bet two thirds full, whilst the gallery presen- ted a most deserted appearance. The Society, with the intention of winking the concert a thorough success, had engaged three well-known artistea of talent, namely, Miss Maggie Davies, wile is evidently a favourite with Runcorn ;nattier:l6es, Mr. Bra xtrin Smith, (tenor) and Mr. David Hughes, (bass). The chorus numbered one hun- dred voices and was under the capable, conductorship of Mr. F. H. Crossley. The chorus in their rendition " By lianyle.n's Wave" (ifetunod), did not meet the ex- pectations of the audience, and exhibited evident signs of weakness. Mr. David Hughes was loudly applauded for his song " Revenge," (fhtton.); and the Aria " Rend?' timm,)," (Soserine) Hamlet; by. Mr. Braxton Smith w4e therorir. appreciated. Macfarrenls cantata . "May Dew " was capitally interpreted 'by the chorus and Miss Maggie Davies, an resulted in lead applause being given to both. T first part. of the programme was brought to a close by the singing of" Thy Foe," (Blumenthal), by Mr. David flughea, who possesses a voic4 of powerful range. The second portion of the proceedings was begun by Miss Maggie Davies and Messrs. Smith and Hughes engaging in the trioentitled The Hawthorn in the glade " (Ben- nett), the pandering of Which called forth from the audi- ence all their enthusiasm, which was manifested by frequent plaudits. Mr. Braxton Smith was encored for his song " Marguerite" (Moir), and responded. A.great snecess was scored by Miss Maggie Davies by her sweet ,singing of " Nella Calms," (Grantor!), for which she watt loudly erreored. • She responded hy singing" My Hugo" in an excellent manner. The chorus gave a ISTaise- worthyinterpretation of thepart song "The Parting Kiss,' and Mx Braxton Smith met with much approval in his contribution "An Evening Song." A second eneore tell to the lot of Miss Davies after singing in a most charm- ing manner the song " Boring," (Henschel). Iler response to this was • happily chosen being the well- known Scotch air " BonninAnitie Laurie,"for witirh she was Tepeatemily applauded. Mr. David ioughes gave a fine rendering of " Hp !Jolly Jertkin " .(Sulliyan). and responded to an encore. The programme was eimi. pleted by the chorus rendering." 1)43-break " (15aning), in a pleasing manner. The singing of the Niti,mai Anthem " terminated the Proceedings. Mrs. W. A. Kty ably accompanied on the piano and Mr.R. Birkett Mus- grove on the organ. •

RUGBY. WARRINGTON V. ROCHDALE HORNETS.

Warrington's opponents for Saturday were the Roch- dale Hornets. It was prophesied that here at air events they were going to be vanquished, because, though being a match for the "Iron men" the previous week, of Bar- row, they could not resist the stings of the Hornets 'of Rochdale'. However, these prophecies were evidently net made bythose who" were in the know," for War.. rington issued from the fray beaming with victory. The Hornets, it will be remembered asserted themselves very effectually when they visited Wilderspool some time age, and this probably accounts for the prophets who follow the Warrington club, being mislea& Severe' reliable players were away from both teams, which were corn_ posed as thus :—Warrington: F. Beesoin, back; C. Potts, J. W. Evans, Cross, and J. T. Massey, three- quarters; James Bate and John Bate (captain;, half- backs; Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, J. Taylor, G. Dakin, J. T. Thorniley, J. Berry, Buckley, and E. Bailey, forwards. linchdale Hornets : Smith, ,back; Wightman, Buckley, Holdsworth, and Isherwood, three-quarters; Howarth and Ogden, half backs; Melledew, Simpson, Dex, Tre- vor, Crabtree, Ashworth, Leach, and Kershaw, forwards. Referee: Mr. W. W. Higgin, Manchester. Turner was deputed te kick off against a slight breeze, and after a brilliant return by Smith, the Warrington forwards at once gave an exposition that was deserving of the higtnat commendation. The Rates passed well, and cross-dribbling by Jolley, aikin, and Berry gave the locals a warm time of it. Free kicks were granted in quick succession, but it was to no purpose. Warrington by the aid of their all-round excellent combination re- newed the attack, which was accurately met by Buck- ley and Wightinan. Another free kick to the home team was followed by Dakin leading the forwards to the line, but by lack of finish a possible chance was lost. The game was dangerously near the Hornets' line, and the Bates, Evans, and Cross tried a passing movement, only to see Buckley (RoChdale) alert, and with the help of Isherwood give temporary relief. Wightman still fur- ther improved the local position, but the respite was of brief duration, for Jolley, Turner, Bailey. and Buckley , rushed the oval back again, and Smith had all his work cut out to keep the eager visitors at bay. Another free kick, taken by Melledew, was more than counter- balanced by Heesom, whilst a couple more penalties , against the visitors were gladly accepted by the hard- pressed Horcets. A round of passing by the home backs was upsettley Massey, and then Taylor, Berry. and Buck- , ley led the way past the RochdalB quarter-flag, Jolley still further improving with a desperate rush, several opponents bringing him down near the line. Isherwood ' kicked luckily and cleared the invaders out, but the Warrin,gtonians' return was indeed disastrous for the ! Hornets. After the Bates had passed finely, a scrimmage was formed near the centre line, and the visitors' front rank heeling cut in quick time, James Bates kicked finely, and Potts racing up at top speed, baffled Smith in fielding the ball, and securing possession, ran in between the posts,the same player placing a neat goal. Dakin, Buckley, and Turner led the way again to the , Rochdale line. and Smith almost let in the Warrington- , ians by a bad miss near, the line. Danger was averted. and Hornets displaying more dash than hitherto rushed down the open for Heesom to accomplish a smart save. Evans, Cross, and.the Bates soon had the locals back at three-quarters, and then by way of a change, Turner took &' free kick, which Holdsworth promptly negatived. A brilliant display by the whole of the Warrington backs was applauded to the echo, Potts being held inside by about a yard. Asworth got the leather away, and then another round of passing by the Bates and Evans were foiled by Buckley and following this came commendable play by Trevor, Simpson, and Crabtree. Dakin led the way beyond the half-wayeonly to see Howarth replv,and for the first time in the match did the Rochdale men assume an aggressive attitude. Free kicks were again granted the locals. and Heesom's charge was menaced. Massey saved splendidly on one occasion, but the home team maintained the attack, and a couple of minutes from call of half-time Wightrnan accepted a pass, and scored far out, Melledew missing thelihot at goal. Half- time score—Warrington, one goal ; Rochdale Hornets, try. With the assistance of the wind in the second half, the game was never in doubt, for direct from the kick- off the locals were kept busily defending. Only once did they pass the half-way flag, and then only for a few seconds, for the fine play of Warrington's backs allowed of no invasion. Melledew restarted the second moiety, and after Jaws Bate had kicked judiciously,the warfare was carried within easy reach of the home goal. Evans and Peits being responsible for the improved position. Potts was almost in from a line out. whilst a minute later he put the finishing stroke to passing by the Bates. only to find the plea of touch-in-goal answered in the affirmative. Efforts by Taylor and Berry resultedin them getting over, but in each case Were the points negatived. Tkis hard luck experienced by Warrington, seemed to have a disheartening effect for a few minutes, and Ogden cleared his lines well, but the visitors, realiz- inc the situation, buckled to, and one screwing of the scrimmage landed them within easy reach of the line. Wild passing by the Rochdale, backs almost let in Cross, and then the Bates electrified their opponents by sharp exchanges, which were spoiled by one transfer being a shade forward. Ashworth and Melledew saved well,and then Ames Bate tricked splendidly, but the opening was lost. Another free kick to Ashworth gave the locals relief, but Dakin dribbled well, and play was again at its original position, Taylor twice over had shots at goal from difficult positions, the last essay being a fine attempt. fieldsworth was floored under his posts, and then John Bate twice was held over the jine. Jolley next %aide one of his desperare rushes and got in, but , the point, was over-ruled, whilst Isherwood in staying the progress of the ceunty forward fell rather awkwardly and dislocated his shoulder. Ogden dribbled the leather away, and passing by James and John Bate saw the former actually getting over, but in his anxiety to make the place eesy he slipped into touch-in-goal, and a minor only was recorded. The visitors increased the pace somewhat now, and after Thornily and Turner had showed up prominently Jolley was floored near the line, but a quick screw of the scrimmage saw Da kin scoring an unimproved try. I 7 the last minute of the match Smith bad a kick charged and Dakin got in again, but a deaf ear was turned to the appeal, and the final result was :—Warrington, a goal and a try (eight points) ; , Rochdale Hornets, a try tthree points.)

WARRINGTON "A " V. ROCIIDALN IiORNBT9 " A."—At Warrington. before a large attendance. The game opened in a rather desultory fashion until a bout of smart passing by the visiting backs forced the home team to defend, a couple of minors being conceded by the defenders. From the drop out Gibson put in a smart kick which was followed by Houghton, Holmes, Hamn- son, and Bandies heading a brilliant dribble right to the Hornets goal. Rochdale, by the aid of Ogden and Brierleat cleared to Warrington quarters. Hammon, Burrov.is,Fairhurst and Woodward transferred hostilities to midfi,irl where splendid passing between Clark, Forster, Lawless, Mannion and Daniels was witnessed. The Hornets were now forced to act on the defensive until a I.olg dribble by Lord, Dearden and Nuttall, carried the leather sphere to the home line. Forster got beautifully away and threw to Clark who repassed to Daniels, the half-way flag being reached. Then Roch- dalwattaeked, Wilcox, Houghton, Holmes and Burrows relieved the pressure and after Lawless had finely scooped tin the ball and saved a dangerous rush, a further minor was conceded. The visitors were still pressing when Burrows came away strongly at halfway, c,oly to see capital play by Brierley and Wood force the Warringtnnians on their line and although having the wOrst of the game, kept their opponents from scoring. With the wird behind them Warringtnn were soon in the visitnrs qoartera,chielly through smart passing between FlF,norasrt:rp,laCylahrvk.ttL:lf!is and Gibson. A loose rush by the Rochdale forwards recovered the lost ground, but Warrington half-backs repulsed the invaders, and a long kick by Roscow rolled dead. The drop out saw the Hornets making an incursion into the home territa-iry. but Mannion put in a huge kick which the visitors fullback mulled, Burrows dribbling over and scoring, from which Lawless placed a fine gnat; Handles, 'Wilcox, Gibson and Burrows were next not ah/e, only to we Ntittall get clear, Lawless flooring him: The warrington halves were playing very well together, Forster being very smart and some capital passing between these two players an Lawless ensued. War- rington were now having considerably the best of the affair, some grand passing between Houghton, Clark. Gibson and Lawless carrying the loather to the visitors quarters. Leach got clear hut a big punt by Manninn sent the warfare to the line where Houghton passed to Handles who scored. Directly after some fine play by Forster and Clark. ended in Lawless scoring, the same player cl.nverting. One of the visitors then got clear and punted, but Forster racing up secured the ball and returned to the Hornets 25 and nothing further being scored Warrington won by 2-1-3 to 0-0-3.

Wmpars V. BLACRT.I4Y.-Thim return fixture was played on Saturday at Widnes, before 1,000 spectators. Black- ley placed thirteen men, and Barber kicked off against the wind and sun. The visitors were the tint to at- tack, and the Widnes lines had very narrow escapes. Drummond eventually brought relief, but only for a minute or two; and then Blackley were again in the home 25. A fine 'passing movement by Widnes transferred the venue, but an excellent chance was missed. A minute or two later, however, Barber rushed over, Drummond failing at the place. The play of Widnw, which up to now had been very poor, improved con- siderably after this succes, and the Blackley defence had all their work cut out to prevent further scoring. Half time score :—Widnes 1 try, Blackley nil. Widney held the upper hand throughout the second half, tries being obtained by Hogan, Darbyshire, and Brennan, the
latter two being improved by Drummond and Barber. Final result :—Widnes 2 goals 2 tries, Blackley nil.

' RUNCORN VICTORIA Y. RUNCORN RECRISATION.—An exciting contest took place between these rival teams on Saturday afterneon, on the around of the former. In the course of the first half Billington a member of the "Recreation "team, had his collar bone broken. He was immediately removed from the field and attended by a medical practitioner. The" Recs." were thus left one man short, but notwithstanding this disadvantage they stubbornly repelled the frequent attacks of the " Vics.." who at the call of half-time had only succeeded in notching a try. On changing endathe wind and sun were in favour of the visitors, who at Once began to make their presence felt and the" Vice.." had anything but an easy time of it. The defence of the latter team was, however, so complete that their antagonists were not able te secure a victory. just once the homesters were allowed to endanger the citadel of their opponents, but the result only ended by their gaining a try. On the other hand the " Recs., ' try as they would, only managed to make a draw of the fixture, the final score reading :—Runcorn Th.-icreation, one try, three minors; Runcorn Victoria, one try, one minor. Sr. Pun's v. HOLT TROTITY.—This match was played on the ground of the former in fine weather. The visitors started and took the ball down the field, but were soon repulsed by the Saints' back. Play was now becoming more of a give and take -nature, till a fine dribble by C. Longshaw, Leach, and E. Longshaw,ended in a goal being scored by Leach, nothing further being scored in the first half. On the ball being restarted, the Saints rushed it down the field, but Jones, of Trinity, effected a grand clearance. St. Paul's no' did did some good pressing, but of no avail, being faulty in the for- wards. Marsh, by a 'sweeping shot scoring the first goal for Trinity. A free kick for St. Paul's ended in a goal being soma for St. Paul's lw E. Longshaw, thus adding number 2. It may be mentioned that Dennett figured very prominently tor St. Paul's. Final result : St. Paul's, 2 goals ; Holy Trinity-, I. WIDNES T. LEIGII.—LANCASIIIRECTSAMPIONSHIP SECOND Cness.—This postponed fixture was played at Leigh on Tuesday before about 3,00 a Spectators. The ground was in a very bad condition. Widnes started against -the wind, and were immediately called upon to defend, but they ynanaired to hold their own for some time. At length Wilding succeeded in scoring a try for Leigli,but the plaee kick was a failure. Two more tries, scored by Evans and Wallwork, were placed to the home team's credit Wore half time, but the goal kicks were failures. Half-time sceres : Leigh, 3 tries; Widnes, nil. Soon after the restart Brennan for the visitors, just missed dropping a goal, but they were credited with a try shortly afterwatds. ,Barber failed at goal. Widnes were now having the best af the play, but they could not break through the home defence. Just before time Wall-' work again succeeded in scoring for the home team. Final score: Leigh,:4 tries; Widnes, I try.

RUNCORN V. ST. HELENS RECRELTION " A " THAM.—Oit Saturday afternoon theabove teams contested for the mastery at Runcorn, before a fairly large "gate." This was a return match, the first having ended in a victory for the homesters by one dropped goal to one try. The visitors were therefore in a determined mood to wipe out this defeat but they were, however, met bp a mood on the part of their opponents which was a determina- tion to add to their formed victories. Play was most. exciting, more especially in the first half. The home team at the interval were leading by one goal, one try, to their opponents nil. During the remainder of the contest play was all in favour of Runcorn, and at the call of time the score stood :—Runcorn, two goals, one try, four minors; St. Helens Recreation, nil.

ST. HELENS RECREATION T. RUNCORN.—These teams met on Saturday afternoon at St. Helens and tried con- clusions before 3,000 spectators. In the first half the visitors had the best of the game, although they were minus the services of Warder, and were successful in scoring a goal. The play during the second portion was of a more even nature, but the score was not ithproved. The final result was :—Runcorn, one goal; St. Helens Recreation, nil.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

PENNITH A.F.O v. WIDNAS.—The first match between these clubs was brought off at Widnes. Play was even for a while, when the home team ran down, and had lines ie not scoring. The visitors .forced nlay to the home goal. N. Parson shot through, but the point was disallowed for off-side. The home team again got away, but bad shooting spoiled some good chances. N: Par- son again scored for the visitors, but the referee would not allow the goal. From a foul in the home quarters Lewis scored for the visitors. Half-time arrived with the score unaltered: On restarting the visitors pressed,, the home goal having many narrow squeaks. The vir4itors kept up the pressure and forced the home back to kick through his own goal. Widnes now pressed for a while' and had several corners to their credit, but failed to take chances. Dykes, who had played a v,obd game dribbled from the centre and passed at the right moment to Bowyer who had little difficulty in scoring. The visi- tors now pressed up to the call of tima. Final result —Penketh, three goals: Widnes, nil. ALL SAINTS V. WARRINGTON PARISH CHARM—Played on the ground of the tatter. The Saints kicked off against the wind and up hill, and after twenty minutes play Gandy scored. This ended the score up to half- time. After change of ends the visiting forwards were soon swarming round the home goal and Landers scored. After this reverse the Parish kiekod well but could not break through the Saints' defence and after Hickens and S. Muokley had shots at goal,tinie was called, the Saints winning by two goals to nil. 01110 RD CRBSCHNT V. PANKIITH (RESBRYI3).—This match was played at Penketh, and resulted in somewhat easy vict-iry for Crescent py four to one. P. Ball scored three goals, and was instrumental ita the scoring of k fourth, which was put throueh by Whiteman. Dutton for. Crescent kept up an invincible defence. Mather and Lawton had hard lines in not scoring.

WIDNES PARISH CHURCH v. RAINHILL.—Thpse teams met at Widnes on Saturday to play their fixture in the West Lancashire LPague. Although the homesters had several of their best players off they played up very pluckily, but were eVencually defeated by three goals to two.

div.head: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.

A meeting of this society was held on Tuesday evening. The balquce sheet of the society was read and showed a dell Cit of £3 17s. 511 The secretary (Councillor A. Bennett) however pointed out that some of the members had not yet paid their sub- scriptions and several members expressed the hope that those who had not vet paid their subsciiptions would do so at once. On the motion of the Rev. E.C.E. Carleton it was decided to fully discuss the matter at another meeting of the society. A paper on" The Church of the Future" was read by Mr. Silcock. In the course of his paper he remarked that it was not for him to:say which was the true church, or to make invidious distinctions between ene or another. The weakest of arguments was to try and exalt one Church at the ex- pense of another. A man's creed did not necessarily make him good, and there were thousands better than their creeds. (Hear, bear.) If a man was had. they rejeced him no matter hoe/ good his creed might be, and if he were proved good, they occepted him no mat- ter by what read he travelled to his goal of moral excel- lence. Ttte church was nearest to God which made the most summer in the world ; that was farthest from Him which made the most winter. (Hear, hear.) • Some men b..rilt magnificent clenches in which to worship, with music at one ,end and a eertain order of service at the other. He did not despise them for it. He cared not what the churches were like, so long as he saw stately christian men coming from them. Then there were bodies which disdained deem ation in their churches,and would not even 'permit music, bodies which despise pomp and :circumstance as much as pomp and circum- stances despised, simplicity.: What did 'it matter, however, if the services of the worshippers 'were good. The churches were merely workshops, the doctrines were the tools, and the memi.tere the workmen. What matter if the shop was cf Oar or of gold if it did not turn out. good Work ? The Chuich of the future would continue to be an ex- ponent and an expreasion of human spiritual experience. The questions were pallid now-a-oars—Was there not evidence that the Christian Faith was beginning to wane? Had the Christian Clkurch come nearly to au end ? If so, had the preaching of the pulpit nr.,thineto do with it? flow many preachers were menaced by the old doctrines and dogmas. Let these men preach about Life and the people would flock to hear them.. The Churches as they existed at present might die but, but religion would not. The Churches were merely the in- struments of religion. A spirit of enquiry was abroad, and it was growing and would continue ts gr)w. There would be a change, but not the least disturbance of the fundamental elements of revealed religion. Despite the doubts of many, he did not know of any time in history when there was a more deep religious faith than that which existed at the present time. There was a ten- dency to believe, a desire to believe, a hunger to believe. They desired a change because the past was too narrow, arid they wished the future to be broader and brbader. The Church of the future would not only be the centre of spiritual enquiry but of petition. Men prayed all the world over. They would continue to meet to worship, and brie representative voice 'Would speak more or less' for all. (Applause.) An interesting discussion followed the reading of the paper. It was taken part in by Councillor A. Bennett, Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, W. H. Drummond, and Messrs. J. Gandy, Douellan, and T. Kent.

WARRINGTON INFIRMARY AND DISPENSARY.
ANNUAL MEETING OF GGVER,NORS.

The annual general meeting. of governors of the Warrington Infirmary and Dispensary was held at the Infirmary on Tuesday afternooh. There were then present : ' Major Pickmere (in the chair), the Rector (Rev. F. W. Willis), Rev. 11. V. Pigot, Rev.W. H. Drummond, Dr. C. White, Dr. Starkey Omith,Dc. Fox, Dr. Richmond and Dr. Bowden (House Sur- geon), Messrs. F..Moriks, C.C., J. White, J. Roberts (Chairman Workingmen's Committee),D. Fanshawe, Geo. Thompson, T. Burton,J. li. Tunstall (hon. sec.), Charles Leigh, G. Dakin treasure;), and Mrs. Pickmere, Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Monks, and Mrs. T. Litton.
TRW YEAIeDACCIDENTS AND DRAMS

Dr. BOWDEN (the house surgeon), submitted his an- nual report is connection with the work of the hotly-it- tion. The report stated that during the year 1893, 343 patient. were admitted to the Infirmary.viz., 322 males and In females.. Among those 18 deaths occurred frera various causes, including three from burns, three from fractured thigh, one from fractured leg, twe from frac- tured skull, one prom wound of aaillary artery, one from poisoned wound of finger. The number of fractures dee t with was 75.. The total armeer of operations was 72. There is an inerease of 74 in the number of patients treated in the Infirmary, of these, 18 deaths which oc- curred, 12. were due to accidents, and inquests were a coroingly held ;of these two patients were so severely burnt that they died: in 341 hours and 7i respectively; three were so terribly injuted that they died will:- in 24. hours of admission; and four were patients aged 68, 70, 74, and 76, respectively. Dispensary :—Out-patients 2992; home patients, 800; accidedts aud emergencies 1318; total, 5110. Among these 154 deaths-occurred. There were 353 more patiemill than last year and the number of deaths 32 more ; the increase in the number of deaths being duo to the pre- valence of summer diarrhoea which carried off large numbers of young ,children and old people. The Dum- ber of fractures treated was 107, and dislocations 10.— Dr.. RICHMOND improposing the adoption of the report said that there was no doubt whatever that the useful- ness of the institution was yearly growing. As a proof of this he mentioned that when he first came to Warring- ton 15:years ago there were 300 cases to be dealt with, while during the present year there had been 1,400.— Mr. George Thompson in seconding the adoption of the report said that he had from various persons who had used the institution, received assurances of the excellent and thoughtful manner in which they, were treated and he thought, taking everything into consideration the Warrington Infirmary could claim to be in good management second to none in the United Kingdom. The report was adopted.

div.head: '2301N ACCOUNTS.
div.p: '2301N ACCOUNTS.

Mr. G6.DARKIN (hon treasurer) submitted his annual statement of accounts. From this it appeared that the income of the institution amounted to £lBl4 17s. 64. and the expenditure £2.56 16s. id. leaving a ditliciency of £24.1 14s. Id. The extension account showed an ex- penditure of £5479144. 7d. against an income of £4212 Ha. 9d. of which £ll3l 13s. 2d. was derived from sub- scriptions.—Mr...l.. Roberts moved the adoption of the accounts and in doing so attriauted the deficiency to the depressed state of trade. In the first place owing to the strikd they had been compelled to abandon the annual concert which generally yielded them about £2O, They had also sustained &loss on the hand contest of £lO ano the subscriptions had naturally been affected by the bad trade.—Mr. BURTON seconded the adoption of the ac- count, and Mr. k. Monks said he thought that the work. lug people did not support the institution so well as they might and he had not doubt that if some means could be arrived at of impressing them with their responsibility towards the infirmary they would gladly subscriiki more generously.—Several other speakers alluded to this sub- ject, and suggested that the Committee should endeavour to induce the employers of labour to interest themselves more in gatharingsubscriptione from the men. ,

MESSRS. WILLIAM JONES AND SON F, OF WA RRINGTON: . •

"The British Trade Journal," of March Ist.,.says : —We had the pleasure of describing in a remit issu.e the various designs of friction hoists manu- factured by Messrs. William Jones and Sons, War- rington. This firm has lately deaigined a new form of steam friction hoist for dealing with comparatively heavy loads, and which, as it presents leatuees: ot nevelty, and will shortly be put upon the market, wilt no doubt prove interesting to buyers ef hoisting machine ery. The main object which Messrs, Jones have in view in their new hoist is, that while it snail be cheap, power- ful, and light, it must be also more rigid and free from i noise and vibration n working than is usual in this.class of work. To secure this condition, the framing is kept low and is of a Strong tee section throughout, all ,pro- '• jections being well bracketed, and the two sides ,ef , the framing firmly tied together by stiff wrought-iron distance pieces. The steam cylinder,. which is strorevJe bolted in a diagonal position onto one side of the fram- ing, is bored to a diameter ofl six inches, and eiaa stroke of seven inches. Time crank-shaft is at,tho top, and it fitted with a cast-iron disc crank and steel, pin. The cylinder is arranged with its steam chest prejeming through an opening in the Me framing, so that the valve gear may be inside the framework and the eccen- tric within ' the bearing. . This arrangement avoids the objectionabeo feature of many hoists which,. through having the eccentric, between the crank and be:wile:7,, -cause a long overhang between the bearingatekerank pin, setting up tarkward strains and vibration, in tee -shaft. The croeshead is arovided with two leng pins, which slide through a suitable bracket and form an efficient and easily-accessible guide for the pistdo 'rod. The,connecting rod is Provided with adjustable gun- metal steps at the crank end, and at the opposite end with a Solid.gun-inetel bush. The crankkshaft at the opposite end Carries, a heavy fly-wheel, and between the bearings, a.friction pinion made from com- pressed paper. Messrs. Jones Sr Sons ha.vo found from long experience that the life of these paper: pinions is practically unlimited.. The second-motion, shaft carries a cast-iron turned friction-wheel. and also 24. spur pinion, which gears •WO a wheel on the barrel sbelt. Tim second-motion Shaft is- mounted at one end in a bearing. block, to which is attached the actuating lever, and which in turn revolv.se in a pedestal placcdteecentrically in such a was, that when he lever is lifted the friction- wheel is pressed ageleist the paper pinioneand, revolving by reason of the friction, causes the weight to be hoisted. When the lever is lowered the. friction-wheel rests by its own weight upon a fixed brake block of hard wood, causing the weight to be suspeneled. Any inter- mediate p.osition,ol the lover permits; of lowering. It will thus be undeestood that this onelever controls every action of the hoist. The barrel on the third-motion shaft is of cast-ironsacid provided with deep flanges to allow for very considerable lifts. A barrel can also be fitted on to the frictioa-wheel shaft if required, and is then capable of dealing with comparatively light weiehte with estreme rapidity. All the bearinge .are two diameters long, and are made separate and bolted to the frames, so that-in the event of breakage they eau easily be replaced. The beerin,gs. for the crank-shafte moreover, have loose caps, for factilitating removal and baking up wear. Ii &fits of this description CAC he made capable of dealing easily with weights up to three tons. They require compara- tively light foundations; and the connectloes are -of the simplest, consisting solely ct wrought-iron steam and ' exhaust pipes. They are admirably adapted for eern mills, textile factories and workshops generally, ware- houses, and docks." An advertisement relating to 'Mrssrs..Jones' patent steam friction hoists will be lound in'anather column..
