"THE POLICE COURT TESTAMENT. Sir,—From time to time I am called upon to give evidence in our Police Court, and it has often struck me on being sworn that the copy of the Testainerit offered for your osculation is certainly not as clean at it might bo. -On Monday week, I was a witness in a ca,e,and had to go throw7h the painful and dangerous ordeal Of kis- sing this dirty copy. Now, as I have to appear in the capacity of witness pretty otten,l give the police autho- rities doe notice that! wiil never again ki,s their dirty backed copy. For it is not (.nly da.ngerou,, as I have said above, hut it is in a measure dis4ra-eful to all concerned. Now, if our police authorities will deign to learn from one so nimble, I would suf,gest a remedy. Why not covfq the book with a white calico cover,which could be washed and changed, say every week? I don't think the cost incurred would increase the rit'?s very rnuch.ani it is simply monstrous and scandalous to ask any respectable person to kiss a book which is in such a vile oondition. Hoping that Mr. Hunt wili see this,and that be will kindly apply the reinedy.—Your., k%, J. C. DALTON. 134 and 133, Bridge-st., Warrington.

THE RIVER AND TILE SHIP CANAL. Sir,—The litigat:on, reported in the " Examiner," be- -I:ween Mesers. Fairclough and the Canal Company ought. I think, to open the eyes of those interested in the well-being of the borough, as to the danger that exists of the detrimental action et' the Canal upon the naviga- tion of the river. I think it must be plain to every thinking person that if, even at this by no means the driest season of the tear, the Canal is taking more than its legal allowance of our river water, it will want more than that when the dry season is upon us. A recur- rence of a season like our last dry summer would result in the silting up of the tidal channel above Runcorn. As a silting agent the tide is our enemy, only to be effi- ciently counteracted by the down-scour of natural drain- age waters. Every gallon of this taken from us is a toss. How will it be when the time comes—as come it must sooner or later—when there is not water em-ugh to supply the needs of both waterways? Will it be the big city and the canal, or the comparatively little town and the river, that will have to give way and suffer the loss of water traffic? The big batallion 13 the one most favoured by Fate. Messrs. Fairclough in this have been lighting the battle of the town as well as their own, and ought to have whatever of help and sympathy can be given in this good cause. While it would be a sin—nay worse, a blunder to unduly hamper the Ship Canal Co., the rights and interests of our town must he zealously safe-guarded. The loss of the river as a commercial water-way would te a sad blow to Warrington. Let the Rivers Cornmitteelook to it.—Truly yours, JOHN PEERS.

SOCIALISM. Sir,—Your correspondent "Common Justice" opens tis remarks in his last letter upon this subject by saying if Mr. Howeroft cares to continue this dientiesion on Socialism, Ste., "There's the rub." I feel that to con- tinue this discussien requires the continual return to old ground, for the greater portion of his remarks this week are already answered by matter I have before eertten. Still, I will endeavour to follow his remarks in your issue of the 3rd. He denies therein that the advo- cates of Socialism are men without property, and -states that the most active and zealous are from the ranks of these who have. Subsequently, lie speaks of individualism being contradictory to the doctrines of Christ. Before he tries to teach me aught of these .doc- trines let him be able to tell me that he and his fellow have so far followed out these doctrines as to have given away all that they had, and can no longer be classed with the " haves." Upon proof of this I shall be dis- posed to listen to him. lam not prepared to be taught doetrinearny teacher does not adopt. To ream to my remarks in a previous letter. I stated that t/ie capitalist had by his thrift enabled the worker t eoduce more by reason of advantageous machinery, ice., thereby cheapening the cost of production, and eventually enabling the labourer to provide the same degree of comfort with a lose expenditure of labour. In eloing this the capitalist sows, and when the time comes to reap the harvest of his foresight, is he to he told tee- the labourer that all the benefits of his improvements belong to labour, and all the capitalist may juetly claim is his own back again? Fancy, the farmer putting a potato into the ground which he hopes in due season may be ten, and when the time comes to gather these ten potatoes he engaees a man to dig them. The man , digs them, and returns to the farmer and ears, " How many potatoes did von put in the ground ?" " One," sacs the farmer. "Here it is, then," says the digger, " you cannot expect more than you put in. The other aline are mine." Now, whatever "Common Justice" may say about the degradation of labour, and as to the higher and nobler aspirations of man being crushed, he cannot get 4way from the fact that man has to work to live, and the system whieh enables him to live with the fewer hours of labour gives greater opportunity for the , development of those higher aspirations. It would be .ratifying to learn something about the higher aspira- tions of this ideal workman of the Middle Ages who rose with the lark and went to bed at dark when he was not /owning in the alehouse, whose children began to work to help to provide the family surtenance as soon as they were fairly out of the cradle, whose oniy thonehts were of working, eating, drinking, and sleeping, whose fond , and dwellings were insanitary, and whose friends. were pestilence and disease. I care not for Pro- fessor Thorold Rogers, Mr. William Morris, or ' Tlallam. The fact remains that numbers of the people where periodically decimated by their insani- tary surroundings, and yet "Common Justice "has the audacity tee tell us they were better fed, better clothed, and better housed. Is it not a fact that we have in this country a higher state of senitation than that of any country of the world past or present, and was it not alleged by German doctors during tke recent cholera ' scare that it could get no effectual hrffd in England ow- ing to the high state of our sanitary arrangements. Again, that the health of the people is better cared fr ia proved by the increase of our population. This proves that the general surrounding' of the people are healthier, and if he wishes for further evidence. in this line is it not a feet that in the town of Oldham alone a matter of L 30,000 is annually withdrawn from saving clubs to en for a week to the seaside. Your man of the Middle Aees was not only unable to do that, hut if he happened to be a serf his property could be seized by the lord of the manor. There are higher ideals than money making says " Common Justice." Yes, but you can do very tittle towards carrying them out without money. The first principle of life, ie to provide sustenance and that sustenance, is best provided by individua.lism where every man has a right to the profit of his own labour. Talk about making the ability of the individual the property of the nation. Bill Smith wreild soon gremble if he found he was doing more work than Tom Jones, and if he could make two pairs of shoes to Tam Jones, one he would want and anght to have mere pay for his extra ability. If he did not get it, he weald lower his production to that, of Tom Jones and Tom Jones would begin to think he was doing above his share and would drop his production else. lam not saying this from theory. This is a thing I have seen at work. The man who by the careful cul- tivation of his talents suceeeds itt eclipsing hie fellow• men is not to be 6rnught down to the level of the man who has neglected his; and the man who can produce more than another has a right to consume more, and if he chose not to consume hut expend it in the manner which facilitates production ne man has a right to begrudge him the harvest of his abilities and labour. lam not aeguing this question on a capitalist line, alone. I say that in its ve-action the nrincinle of *locialiem would act unfaveurahly on the masse, for it is by the development of the ability of the individual owing to a foreseen gain for himself that the masses are benefitted. " Did Carlyle and Emerson tile ther Zies merely for their own advantage," save" Common Justice." Well just in the same manner as I deecribe they benefitted themselves and the public ; as Stenhen- son ,Davy, Bessemer, Themes and Gilchrist. Sicanens,and a host of others, have done. The benefit to the nehlic eame by first benefitting the individual. Oer friend eave we should have had Darwin's researches if lie hae imat tnonev by them, and I say that if Darwin had not he- tongeif to that class, of which "Common Jiieriee e„e they reap where they do not ?ow, we should not, have ha 4 his researehea at all, and Ruskin it is probah'e would have been similarly situated. As te Boman generals, their services were at the service of the nation hut the price of a general and that of a soldier differed. You have not adduced a single reference Mr. "Cum- men Justice" which supports your arguments, every in- stance you have given is a proof of the ether side. Let - me here remark Mr. " Commoa Justice" I am not to he neenced with untruths, and when you say that the Soeialist is not hostile to the foreigner, and he only de- slairna against the influx of foreign labour, became such labour is exploited to bring down the standard of wages, you say that which is contrary to fact. I ran lay my hands on scores of young Germans who came over here of their own accord, because they believe the con- dition of the worker here is better, and also the possibi- lity of advancement greater. " Why did you come here, Karl," said I to one the other day, " Dia anyone _bring you over to take someone else's Place." "No," said 'ne, " I came over because I believed I should mend my- self, and that I was justified is proved by my staving, and I can tell you I don't mean going hack this fall." I know none who have been brought here lir the capita- list. but I know a few who have come because their friends have advised them to. Many of the Jews in London have, it is true,been assisted over to Lendorenot to pull down the price of le hour, but because the coreli- tions of life, even to such wretchedly paid people were better in London than from where they came. -
T. Y. HOINCROFT.
Middlesb,)ro', MArcli 12, 1894. DOES SOCIALISM MEAN SELFISHNESS?

Sir,—ln a recent issue of the "Examiner" appeared a letter signed by T. Y. Havvcroft. Inasmuch as the letter referred to is not written in a spirit at all conducive to " real Socialism," I might be excused from giving it notice, but I prefer rather to again do something to- wards malting T. Y. El. a useful and ilet a harmful member of society. . _ .

I am soinewhai at a loss to know where the selfishness of Socialism comes in. That is, the selfishness that is objectionable, and to which T. Y. H. refers. Is it selfish for the people to wish to own the railways,the telegraph, and the teephone ? If we find the ownership of these features in business working well for the whole people, ! would it be still more selfish to aim at owning the water works, the gas works, and the electric light? If, after the possession of these aids to social life, we find the people satisfied they have not made a false step,nor even Aded a selfish trait to their character, they should, like Oliver Twist, ask for more, would 'l'. Y. H. object, and do a little more" probing " ? Which is the most selfish, the capitalist who refuses to pay a "living wage" to the collier, and who sacrificed on the altar of competi- tion during 1893 one thousand and fifty-six lives, or the Socialist who demands that the earth and the fullness thereof shall belong to the nation, and not to the indivi- dual ? Is it not clear to all that so soon as competition has forced coal owners to say that the getting of coal 'does not pay," that it will then be followed out on new conditions which must be either by the formation of a company, as suggested by the late Sir G. Elliott, or by the taking over of the whole of the minerals at the price competition has reduced thenl to? I would, with all patience, ask all objectors to the . trend Socialism is taking,to take up the study of any one of England's great industries, either the factory system, • coal getting,or agriculture,and they will then know how much of value there is in T. Y. Ff.'s words,—" By eco- nomy and care the capitalist has given the coentry the power to purohase more with fewer hours of labour." We are told that "it is by people living below their in- come that machinery has developed." Such nonsense could only be put forward by one in complete ignorance of the romance of trade. The father of T. Y. H. lived in the same town and worked at the same trade with one who never in his life lived below his in- come, and who started in business with other peoples money,and who now bids fair to be a millionaire. Given a man with good business qualities and the ability to I exploit his fellows, and you have success. The " real Socialist "never raises his voice against the capitalist per se, lint it is against the system that creates capitalists. Let us look a little deeper into this. A capitilist, and one with whom we are all acquainted, and whose picture I am pleased to h, ng in my room, 1 did, a number of years ago, a somethine which some might call Quixotic, but which really spriieg from hif, • love of his fellowman. He urged his fellow workmen to club together and purchase a large business property then standing idle. Time has proved that he well knew his own business capabilities, and that in offering them to the men he was offering something of priceless value to them, as well as to himself. His advice was rejected. This was over thirty years age, the works stand idle to-day, but the would-be saviour of his fel- lows tilted no more against wind mill sails, but went for somothing more substantial, and to day he has the big- gest public monument in Warrington, besides some- thing that represents his personal energy. T. Y. H. says wages ars 40 per cent, higher to-day than they were in his younger days. In answer to this I have only to refer him to the methods of working, and to the price lists of his own trade. More on that I cannot say with- out being personal. A reader of Socialistic literature has read to little pur- pose if the outcome is a belief that Socialists " oppose capital as being injurious to the worker." I think that is a position the Socialist would not take up, as being fruitless. Tito Socialists methods are constructive, hut let UR look how far the development of capital benefits the worker. lam now studying the report of the recent Royal Commission on Women's Labor and Wages, and I find that women are now employed in the manufacture of bedsteads, buckles, and boots, nails, nuts and bolts; at the latter working 56 hours a week they are paid 4e. 61. Thoy also atteral furnaces, and move and load fish plates on the railway lines f •.r which after working 56 hours they receive 43. 6d. as a proof that they are better off than their dear dead and gone sisters of the past were. Truly capital is a God before whom we all ought to worship. IF willing, T.Y.I. may now look with me over the report of the Welsh Land Commission and he will find that there does exist to-day people who do not, and cannot rest and he thankful because "We are better off than at any other period or the coun- try's history." Amon, the picturesque features of Lard Stanley of Alderley's evidence are the following :
":,r, far as I am avrare,gamekeepers aro the best friends of tha tenantp.

Here in Wales labourers are decidedly well off. I think they are too well off, because where the labourer is boarded and lodged it is quite unreasonable that he should get 10-i.a week besides. I ttave conctantly Peppered dogs at a distanee. I don't remember shooting, one belonging, to my tenants to kill it, hut I never see a dog in a field without hla zing at it more than a hundred Yards or so. That is the only way of impressing upon the dogs and upon farm ser- vant; what is proper." The latter half of T. Y. H.'s letter is too ranch for what small amount of gray matter there may he in rni; brain, as, for instance, will he explain the following." I have no regard for a man who has sought every oppor- tunity in the columns of the " Examiner" to run down the cause of temperance." lam not at all anxious to know the meaning of this, but I am anxious to gain the regard of one who has always "been content to live on the wage of the majerity of the workmen around him." I think it will occur to most people on reading the above that, after all, there may he something in Socialism worth looking. into. The ideal it is aiming at will not even he nut further off by the traverstips of ea reless critics, such as the Rev.E.C.E.Carleton and T. Y. H. I propose' t. deal with the first of these candid friends in a future letter. In the meamtime I should like to know who has said, and in what place has it been said, that " Social- ism proposes to give everybody the same wage." This is mere nonsense like a heap of other things that are laid to its e.harge. Socialism recognises that the capitalist %in. and does, pick the brain of the genius in whatever walk of life he may anrear. A thousand instances of this might he given. Milton writing his for a paltry Goldsmith writing rubbish beeinge of his poverty. Painters without number in the hands of picture dealers. Since the days of James Watt inventors without number have bent before capital only to sink into early graves. Socialism would nurse and reward tbese men to the well-heing ef society. Everything that is bright, and good will he develoned by !ocialisin, hilt never by selfish individualism, and so the individuality of ;Irian pre- served.--Yours, Sze.,
Northrit!eA. wnrrAster, Feb. 16. 1894.
H. winrrilv,

Sir,—l am sorry to trouble you again on this subject hut Mr. Peers will bave it so. Yes: I hr,th said that the seed had a soul (animcei, and also denied that the same had a conscious life. I should have thought that both propositions were self-c.vident, but it seems they are not to your corr.spondent. The soul (in se) simpfr means, the life principle, etrrnal, undvine., never•ending ; and this I think Mr. Peers and your other correspondents admit applies to the seed. But this term does not predicate cons7ions life, and it says little for Mr. Peer's accuracy and discern- ment that he did not knew it. The term conscious life applies only to man, and materiali,ts would have ns be- lieve that this conscious life with its envn:ope, is anni- hilated when the change called death takes place. The,. only ditiererp-es between the soul of the seed and the human soul, is that the former is buried with its enve- lope. and the latter is not, but is external to it. ho' to suzu.vest that these f,,,entietren who are in doubt about these "perplexing problems" shonld— headed hy Mr. Peers—visit the parish priest of Warring- ton, and courteously ask him to else them a. course of lessons on metaphysics—or ethics and natural law finishing up by a coursedf logic.—Yours JOFIN S. Sir,—This cnntroversy has bren very interesting end has given to your very many rearlers much nleastire, something new to read and to think about ; v-hich is a btegsing not to he despised. Accordingly. I tender tn Harry Esmond, the proposer of this perplexing question, and ynnr other correspnridents who have taken it up so heartily, my very hest thanks. I will, with your kind permission, try tn make the hitherto losing side, look a little better. First of al!. I will read the text containing the words in nispnt,A.with. out using the pronouns, which is as follows : " Except a corn of wheat fall into the 2round and die, this n•rn of wheat abideth alone ; hut if this corn of whost die this corn of wheat hringeth forth much fruit." I have written the text in this manner bec4 use some 0, e your onrrospon- dents thought it was only nart of a grain, as for instance " external wranpinns,"" integuments." and " investi- ture," all these were to die. I do say that I wonder how all these things got into the text. Then Mr. J. Peers in yours of March the 3rd, when he was roasting Ben Chayil said, that this corn of wheat ." could only mem
the embryo." This was news! precious news only to no I had from renketh ! ! There are several "its" iu the text which may account tor these extraordinary things.

Christ said "-that if a corn of wheat fall into the pound and die, it bringetk forth much fruit." The world denies this and declares that if the wheat die there will be no issue. For once let us throw books and opinions on °use side and hold, as Bacon says, uninter- rupted intercourse with nature. First, the corn falls in- to the ground ; secondly ,something cometh up ; this something is not tlic seed ; fourthly, the seed is riot in the ground. Query. Where then is the seed ? It , has departed this life. The corn of wheat contains latmt life ; also something to support life ; that is to say first principle. This latent tile is not for the use of the seed, but the seed, or corn of wheat, holds this latent life in trust for the benefit of the prospective wheat plant. Did I say held in trust ? Yes, sir, and well this trust is kept, for it is a matter of history that wheat has been kept tor thousands of years. It has then been sown—to render up its life to set young plants agrowing ; yea, and they did grow. The habits of plants are various, so if we look round we may get something relating to the knowledge we seek. Some have their seeds in the ground like the wheat, whilst others bring up the greater part of the seed as they grow from the ground. Cabbage seed per- sue the latter course. It comes up split in two on a tiny stalk one half turns to the right and the other half of the seed turns to the left, and they become two little leaves. Plants in this condition are called " seedlings " but this is not exactly the proper name because, though these " seedlings" come direct from cabbage seed, they are not cabbage plants, but are a sort of nurse-form made for the rearing and protection of the true cabbage plant. In the intermediate space between these two seed-leaves there is a little cup or hollow formed in which a little speck soon becomes visible and as this rises it proves itself a bud which swells and grows and then a cabbage plant appears. But note just as this bud begins to un- fold and its leaves to spread, the nurse-form—thr,se seed- ling leaves which had been the veritable seed die and ' fah off. Why did the nurse-form die ? Because the true cabbage plant absorbed its life. Here the seed dies after becoming a nurse-form but the plant lives. In digging up young potatoes how often do we find a good crop where the seed potato is not only dead but rotten ? The seed dies but the plant brings forth abun- dantly. Mr. John Peers writes as if the seed contained the plant, but can a plant live for a thousand years , without air and without water ? Then, again, he says, • "The embryo does quicken without any tart of the grain dying." The embryo has no existence till quickening takes place,and it is the result of the quickening. Quick- ening takes place when the corn of wheat has taken in enough of water and of heat to stimulate it to action, then the embryo is begun. Now, as this embryo is to become a living plant, where is it to get its life from ? From the seed, as it can come from no other source. In other Words, thelseed enriches the embryo with the life which nature has treasured up within it. Therefore, it has lost its life and is dead. "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone ; but if it die, it bringeth forth.much fruit."—Yours, &c.,

FELIX SUMMERS. P.S.—lt is the psssing of life from the seed which kills it, and it is the reception of that life b 7 the embryo that r.alres it to grow and to " bring forth much fruit."—F. S. [The correspondence on this subject is now closed.—En. "Ex."]

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 17, 1894
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 17, 1894
THE TOWN CLOCK.

Sir.—l should not think it worth while to reply to Hickory Dickory's letter in your last issue were it not that I feel bound to counteract as far as possible the eff•ct of his unjustifiable refle,ctions upon the accuracy of the town clock. He brings forward no evidence in support of his contentions, and does not pretend to have made any systematic observations of the clock; but makes sweeping assertions and unwarrantable supposi- tions, leading off with the following startling statement, that" at present the public clocks of Warrington are scarcely worth more than the dignity of being kitchen monitors—something by which to boil potatoes;"—a nice compliment to the donor of the town clock. To those who know the truth about the clock,this assertion simply proves one of two things, either that Hickory Dickory has taken no notice of it, or that whet, he has chlrie so he has not known the correct time. To mak.-! such assertion without positive knowledge of its truth deserves censure, considering that the interest of the public are involved. lam not aware that anyone has ever claimed that the town clock can be depended upon to give Greenwich mean time within one second,or even within ten seconds ; but I do maintain that, as it is rarely more than quarter minute wrong, it has a good ckiin to be considered reliable—something better than a kitchen monitor. Like all clocks Ido not doubt that it requires occasional regulation to keep it winin bciinds.

Passing on to the next paragraph of Hickory Hickory's letter we meet with two statements which,as specimens of cool assertion, would be hard to beat. EI6 writes as follows : "he (1,. W.R.) has not a watch than can be trusted to carry the time from the landing stage to Warriwqon within 0.25 sec., nor had he got true time so near as that,could he tea the stroke of the hour to so flee a degree." I have nowhere asserted that I can carry the time from Liverpool t* Warrington without the pos- sibility of error arising from variation of my watch, but even had I made such an assertion, Hickory Hickory would have no right to flatly contradict me without ' knowing something of the quality of watch I carry. I am sufficiently familiar with its rate to justify nay say- ing that the errors in any observations, arising from var- iation of the watch, are not likely to exceed and that if the clock were always observed at 2 p.m.,that is ars hour after hearing the gun, they would in most cases be well within isec. That my flz,ures cannot be far from the truth is proved by the fact that a friend who carries a watch shnilar to my own and also notes the errors of the clock, obtaining his time from a different source, arrives at nearly the same results as myself. Our estimates seldom differ by more than a second ,our obser- vations being made, not on the same, but on consecu- tive days. As to noting the time of striking to Fee, I suppose I must conclude that a "feat of horological ac- curacy "of which Hickory Hickory is "as yet inean- able," is nec.essarily impossible. All I can say further on this point is that anyone with good eye-sight who is unable, by carefully watching the second hand of a watch, to note to a Fee., tll9 time when an expect-A sound is heard, must possess a dull. faculty of percep- tion.

Hickory Dickory next proceeds to suggest that the clock may vary irregularly and that, although right on the dates I mentioned, it may have varied between times, also that we do not know how often the clock may have been altered in the intervals. I fail to see what useful purpose is served by suggesting mere nossi- bilitita. The first questicn Hickory Dickory Plight ilaVf! settled himself, had he taken the trouble to observe the clock ; and if the result had proved unsatisfactory, it would then have been soon enough to write to the local papers and endeavour to shake public confidence in the clock. As to the second question, I have ascertained that the clock was not altered once during the period covered by ma' record ; that, in fact,it is very rarely ever corrected excent by regulation. If hickory Dickory unders.ands the principle of the gravity eseapement, used in all the best turret clocks, he ought to know that anV serious irregularities in such clocks can only occur as the result of accident or neglect. I lived for three years within hearing of the town clock, rarely missing a nay without noting its time, and I compared it two or three times a week with the Leigh time-signal without perceiring any tendency to irregular time-keeping. I used also to compare it daily with a Vienna reeallator,to which I have fitted a mercurial ;:ompensated pQndulum, and it was most interesting to note the uniformity of ! variation between the two clocks. I have no objontions to raise to your corresnondent's remarks about Russell's regulator, except that they are not to the point. The question at issue is whether, or not, the regulator is sufficiently accurate to serve as a test of the town clock's reliability. and lrivin.-; consulted it. weekly f...r a period of two months and found its error almost invariably less than 3 5M.7.5., I think it not. unrea- sonable to conclude that it may be tru.ted for the pur- pose suggested. The remainder of hickory Dickcry's latter requires no comment as it does not concern the town clock, hut I most not omit to thank him for the friendly wish exnref,sed in his eoncluding sentence, up:m which I should like to remark that such letters as his afford one little encouragement to continue sending records of the clock's rate to the 1"cal pap drs, also that if he supposes I have only rec-ntly begun to observe the town click, he is tinder a wrong impression. I havo closely for ten rears, that is almost from the time of its erection in 1883, so I mac fairly claim the right to speak with some authority on the subject. This is the second time I have been drawn into a controversy nn this subject. On the first oc.lasion, some years ago, it was with a correspondent of the " Guardian." who eventuallr admitted that he had taken no notice of the clock. "rot caring to submit myself to the inconveni- ence of having to reply to the correspondents who win nor tale.- the trouble to ascertain the truth for themselves I shall in futore refrain from pulishng any further statements about th.e clock's at —Yours. k.c., F. W. REYNOLDS, P..A.

P.S.--in Pcsertiwz the pr.s,ihility of noting VI,. time of strikinsr to fit:4l. I don't wish t ) Unuly that 1 thiNk it worth while to h. so eKant, or that 'I pretend to estimate the clock's error o to such a degree of nicety.
THE DF4ET crnATRITM ENT AND DTSENDOW- -34 ENT OF 'PUP, CDURCII OF ENGLAND.

Sir,—l notice that tho IVarrington Dehatin.Y, Society at its me,,joa on Tuesday v.veek, en:zae 1 in diH-- cussin,! this most important subjeat, and that notwith- .stardinz the cast amount of information which has from time to time been furnished on the question. the essatist (Mr. Plirst,on) was ty:i 1 cm-inch to declare th,t " The Church of Erwland was never, as was corninonlv asserted by Dic4,,nters,estalli,hecl hy Act of Parliament." fie also gaud. With ree•ard to the Eridowtrents (f the Church of Encdand, it could not riczhtfutly he said that they belon,ed to the nation ; they had hcen the sponta- neous gifts of the sons of the church for hundreds of years past." To which church rhaeA he refer ? The onr, Iv law es- hlichcd Rt the Pr,forrratior, r-r the Pomi,zh Church, which exited in Enfrland for s th-usand yems t-efore tLat period, which ackn.owledged thkl Pope as As head,

and which I maintain) in spite of Mr. Arthur Bennett's denial) was not ideajcal with the State Church of the present day ? In support of this contention the great majority of historians and writers of ecclesiastical history are agreed upon this point. Mr. Freeman sa7s (" Fort- nightly Review," September,l37l) :—" Betwcen British and English Christianity there is absolately no conti- nuity. British Christianity is first displaced by English heathendom,and it is then conquered by the Christianity winch England learned direct from Rome." Mr. G. W. Child, M.A., in the introduction to his " Church and State under the Tudors,"strongly insists that the church in England was in no true sense "national," but was completely identified with the western church under the authority of Rome. The Bishop of Liverpool says (Prin- ciples for Churchmen,lBB4l) :--"The three hundred ears which immediately preceded the Reformation is a period when the Church of this land was thoroughly, entirely, and completely Roman Catholic, when the Bishop of ;Rome was the spiritual head of the church ; when Ro- manism reigned supreme from the Isle of Wight to Berwiek-on-Tweed,a rid from the Land's End to the North Foreland ; when the ministers of religion in England and the people were all alike Papists." Such was the condition of things up to the time of that historical " Blueheard," Henry VIII., when (as the result of the quarrel between that monarch and the Pope on the subject of the king's divorce and his mar- riage with Anne Boleyn) by the Acts 26 Henry VIII. c.l and 35 Henry VIII. c. 3, the king was made head of the " Church of Eraland," and that was the Roman Catholic Church, not the present establishment. He also, by various Acts of Parliament, confiscated the monasteries and possessions of the Church, which have thus became state property. Surely, this is not the property which the present State Church claims—in the words of Mr. Plinston and Mr. Bennett—as " the spontaneous gifts of the sons of the church for hundreds of years ).)ast." Now mark, Mr. P., during the next rtig,n we see the passing of an Act of Parliament, making the present "Protestant Church of England." By the Acts 2 aud 3 E Iward VI. chapter 1, intituled " An Act for the uni- formity of service and administration of the sacraments throughout the realm," which sets forth the various rites and forms of worship to be observed'' in any cathedral or parish church,or other plaee, within this realm," and also the punishment by fine or imprisonment of all per- sills who did nor comply with the law, and thus by this Act was created the law estalli3hed church,known as the Protestant Church of England, an Act threatening pecuniary ruin, restriction .f freedom, and ejectment of Catholics from their benefices unless they became apostates from the religion of their ancestors (whose " spontaneous gifts had been given to their church for hundreds of years past,") and conform to the newly. created State Church.

_ Sir, it ill becomes the defenders of a church founded on such a basis, to describe the advocates of religious equality as " spoliators and robbers," because of their desire to participate ia the benefits to be derived from this "national property" to which we have—even in our own times, been compelled to contribute. I know it is an old cry that the Church is not one penny the richer because of its connection with the State. I also know that it is an untrue one, and hundreds of thousands of pounds have been given by Parliamentary grants,and in the remission of dutit,s on materials used in the erection of churches—these privileges being denied to Dissenters. Indeed,in this town of Warrington there stands a church which cost over £s,ooo—and of this sum more than Z.,/, OW was contributed by the State towards the cost of erection, and over £94 duty remitted from the mate- rials used in building—and yet, forsooth, we are told Ma', the disestablishrnent and disendowment of the Church of England is desired by p9rsons who want that which does not belong to them.—Yours,
HISToRICCS.

div.head: BAZAAR AT HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHAPEL.
div.p: BAZAAR AT HILL CLIFFE BAPTIST CHAPEL.

For the purpose of raising funds towards liquid- ating the expense recently incurred in improving the Hill Cliffe Baptist Chapel buitdings, a bazaar was opened on Thursday at noon. The schoolroom —in which the bazaar wart held—has had its some- what sombre_and quaint interior transformed with quite a galaxy of fanciful designs arid ornamenta- tions, work which had been done by a committee of young men and young ladies, with materials kindly lent by Messrs. S. E. and It. Johnson. The attendance at the opening ceremony was as large as the outiding could accorninotiat.e, and among those present were : Mr. A. Burrows J.P. (Moderator of the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Association of Baptist churches) ; Mr J. W. Schofield, J.P., of Bootle, Mr. F. Monks, C.C. J.P, the Rev. J. S. Hughes (pastor), the Rev. J. W. Varley, mi Rev. D. W. Roberts, and Messrs. J. Longland,Bailey flarrixon, Dsvies (Lymm), J. Hough, and W. Hougn (Onston), and a number of ladies. Alter short devo- tional exercise.

The Rev. J. S. EittaHEl called upon Mr. Burrows te open the bertar. In doing so he said that when he came to Hill Chi& some five months ago he soon found that I the atmosphere was strongly charged With bazaar germs I which were especially numerous about that excellent !restitution the sewing class. (Laughter.) He thought it aemewhat unfortunate for his ministry to be attended in its opening by an epidemic sn lie did all he could to Seep awey from the germs. (Laughter.) But in spite of all his precau:ions the epidemic grew. and ist about , two months everyone was suffering from a more or less serene; attack of ttle bazaar fever, which had then to be allowed to have its way,and which he had been informed would come to the crisis about neon that day. (Renewed laughter.) Aft -r a few more facetious remarks, the speaker said that the bazaar had been organised for the purpose of raising a fund to help to defray the cost of renovating the chapel. They would notice that much had been olone to the building, and in addition to some rebuilding they had supplanted the old square-backed pews—which eeemed to have been good enough for their straight-laced ancestors—with more modern and .cninfortablis pews. This work had involved an expenditure of some £750 towards which they had received £5OO, and there now remained in consequence £2OO to be defrayed. He wished to mention) that there existed an error in respect to the , temporalities ef the church. It was corm-I:wily rutneured that Hill Cliffs Church was very richly endowed, and in conseqaence quite a number of persons had declined to sub-.cribe to tee improvements. lie wished to contra- dict this rumour, and to state that with tise exception of £2O or £3O per annum derived from the grave yard,they had to ineet all the expenses of the place with funds re- ceived front generous members of the congregation. (Hear, hear.) He was very glad the Church was not ' endowed, because he thmieht endowed Churches were not so useful as they might be. (Applause.) In cenclu- eion the speaker aeluded to the historic connections of the Church and said that as the first home of Noncon- formity in this locality, it (melt to receive such support from the Nonconformists generally as would enable its managers te erect, if net a cathedral—at least a build- ing more suitable to the traditions of the site. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Burrowe, after a few well chosen renserks,declared the bazaar opened, and a vote of thanks for his atten- dance was accorded him on the motioia of Mt. Schofield, seeended by Me. F. Monks. The sales were then proceeded with. The following are the names of the etalltiolders :—No. I. stall : Mrs. Kenworthy, Mrs. Booth, end Miss Arnold. Ni. 2 stall : errs. Hell, Mrs. Dodd, and Miss Booth. No. 3 stall: Mrs. lirminde, Mrs. Timperley, Mrs. Mether, and Miss MOM Ne. 4 stall : Mrs. Arnold, Miss 15.0,011, Miss Horton, Mrs. D irhvshire, and Miss E. Kenworthy. Market stall: Mrs. Au:ea-ell and Mrs. John Bradford. Refreshment stall : Mrs. Longhand, Miss Bradford, end Miss Harri- son. Refreehinent rooms : Mrs. Lamb, Miss Kenworthy, Miss L. Kenworthy, and Miss Strange. Book and News stall : Rev. J. S. if eehes, Mr. Joseph Moss, and Master Hughes. The Illy superinteedents of the bazaar were Mrs. Hu turdghes ed 'Mrs. Braelferd. In the evening a vocal and instrumental concert was given in the chapel. An interesting programme was eene trough, end there was a very large attendance. The following artistes took part: Pianoforte solos, Miss Boardman and Miss Derbyshire ; songs, Mr. A. Grounds, Mies Bastter. Miss Fieldhouse, Miss Timperley and Miss D. Feet violin solos., Miss D. Hall ; and cornet solos.. Mr. "Meredith. The preceeds for the day amounted to £lO5 174. 80. On ^Friday the bazear was opened by Miss Bessie Duteon. There was again a large attendance.—The Pastor he introdneme Miss Dutton said that he was glad to say that everything had passed off very successfully ! n:t thf. previous dee. The attendance had been larger I than they had tiered to anticipate, the sales had been I very numerolis, and the concert had been exceedinely successful. He was therefore happy to state that they were now much nearer the object they had in view,than I they were the previous day. They were still £l5O short Of what they wished to ohtain, however, to clear off all reepensibility. They had the pleasure that day of having to open the pro- ceedings, a noble, gifted lady, who had done much work in connnectinn with Christian causes in the neigh- bourhood. He heartily welcomed her among them. (Apeleuse.l lie was eled that in her they haiii.a mew- ter of the Wvslevan body, which showed that although they were in the unfortunate position, of having the baz,ter at the same time as the Wesleyan fr:ends at BolJ- st, still there was no rivalry between them.—Mies Dutton thanked Mr. Hughes and the friends at Hill Cliff,. for asking her to be present that day. She had just been in the chaeol adjeinine, ;led was glad to see so many improvements. The chapel was wonderfully effi- cient for the purposes of worship,end was very different to when she saw it a few years ago. She was glad to see se many present and to see the walls so beautifully decorated. It was a'credit to those who had done such self-denying work to make the bazaar a success. She hoped the bazaar that day would be a great succes.—The Rev. W. J. Kirkland, of Warrington, moved a vete of thanks to Miss Dutton for her presence that day, and wished prosperity to the Church.—Mr. Longland, in I seconding the motion, spoke of Miss Dutton's readiness to take part in all good work in Werrington and neigh- bourhood.—The motion was unanimously passed. Miss Dutton suitabiv replied, and the bazaar was then de- clared open.—in the evening another successful concert was given in the chapel, there being a largo number of artistes present from Warrington.

div.head: ATHLETICS.
div.p: ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

The Warrington team continued their victorious course on Saturday, their latest victims being Rochdale Hor- nets, whom they vanquished by eight points to three, after a most one-sideo game. One of the features of the match was the number of times in which the Warring- ton players crossed the line, and had tries disallowed. They crossed no less than ten times, and on only two of these occasions were the scores permitted. There is something wrong here, and it, must have had a very dis- heartening eff,-ct upon the • s. The Hornets must have deteriorated or the Was :),ngtonians must have vastly improved since the first match which was played between the two teams, for on that occasion, the Hor- nets' forwards fairly ran away with the Warrington for- wards, and it was only the safe defence that kept them out. At the match on Saturday, the Warrington for- wards were superior as were also the backs.

During the match, Heesom had very little chance of showing what he could do, for his set viees were scarcely ever in requisition, in striking contrast with Smith of the opposite side who was continually at work, and came out of the ordeal very creditably. Cross ot Stock- ton Heath, made his first appearance in first class matches on Saturday, and he helped to emphasize the fact that Stockton Heath is a wonderful place for rear- ing excellent three-quarter backs. In fact, I believe the whole of that department could be filled very creditably from that part of the country, which shows that ‘Var- rington has no fear of a dearth of three-quarters for some time to come. "Smack" Bate signalised his reappear- ance in the team by combining with his namesake John, and completely over-masterirg the " Insects" halves. Jolley worked like a Trojan, and why he as not yet received higher honours than county -honours, I cannot understand. - The rest of the forwards had their full, share in the victory.

To-day ic played the "match of the season." The Lions of Swinton are due this afternoon at the Wilders- pool enclosure, and as the Warrihgtonians are in such excellent form, a grand game will be witnessed. A great deal depends upon this match. Should Warrington win, they will take the second place in the league, as they are at present only one point behind Swinton, though of course Swinton have a match more to play. Another circumstance which should put zest in the Warrington play is that they have a chance of inflicting the first defeat upon Swinton in this season's league matches. Not a single club in the league which has yet met Swinton either at home or away, has been able to accomplish this feat. Warrington came very near to it at Swinton when they scored the first try in the match, but Swin- tan at length drew level. The Warrington ground has been a fatal ground to the hopes of the Swintonians in the majority of cases, so that I shall expect to see War- rington come out on the right side on Saturday.

By the way, is it not unfortunate that Warrington should have suffered such a narrow defeat at Oldliatn ? Had they won, they would now have headed the leagu9 table with one point ahead of Oldham and Swinton, and an almost certain chance of the championship. It was said at the time that the match was an important match, but no ono thought it was of such paramount importance as it has now proved to be, for it may result in Oldham gaining the championship. However it is of no use "crying over spilled milk," and Warrington must now look to next season for a chance of getting to the top of the competition although they have still a good chance of coming in second.
From the followinz table it will be seen how the com- petition at present stands :

The international matches in which Ireland has been eng,aged have now come to an end with the result that the Emerald Islanders have carried off the international championship. This is an astonishing feat, for last year ini•tead of winning,they lost all the matches they played, thus following the example of Wales who also accom- plished the same transformation from " wooden- spoonbits" to champions. The Irishmen have only had narrow victories,the match en Saturday with Wales only being won by a penalty goal, but still they have been enouzh, and a little more retpect will be given to the Irish forwards, and to forward play in general in con- sequence. •

The team chosen for the match against Swinton, to- day, is of the following composition: Heesom, full back ; Broady, Potts, Evans, and Barber, three-quarter hacks; S. Bate and J. Bate, half backs ; Turner, Jolley, Nevins, Buckley, Thorniley, Barry, Taylor and Dakin, forwards. Bailey is down as reserve man.

I hear that Mr. G. P. Dewhurst, of Oughtrington Hall, Lymm, has signed a league form as an amateur for Liverpool P.C., and will most likely play with that club towards the close of the present season. Mr. Dewhurst has this season been playing for the Old Corinthians and Liverpool Ramblers,and has for the past four years turned out with the Cambridge eleven-against Oxford. He has also on occasions assisted the Lymm Football Club.

div.head: BILLIARDS.
div.p: BILLIARDS.

E. Diggle and E. Bancroft are, I hear, coming to the Conservative Club next Saturday (the ath) to give an exhibition. Diggie is the champion of the North, and Bancroft the champion of Liverpool. Ihe game will be 2,060, Bancroft receiving a start of 750. Diggle is just now in splendid form, as will be seen from the reports which have appeared of his match with Peall at Manchester.

div.head: BOATING.
div.p: BOATING.

A week to-day (Saturday) there will he decided the great question of "Who will win the boat race 9" lam a very indifferent prophet or I would shy off a few pro- phecies ; hut one has to be a very knowing sort of person to even give beforehand, a shrewd guess at the winner. In the first place,much will depend upon the wind, and in the second place, much will depend upon luck in the last part of the race, where as a rule, people's expecta- tions are generally shattered by the unexpected develop- ments.

The boats are eKoected down at Warrington by 1 p.m. " Pink " has the first start, while " Gipsy " is down at scratch. The three new boats to which I made allusion last w•-ek, will be watched with much interest. The officials for the race are :—Mr. J. Wicklow, judge ; Mr. F. Truscott (number taker), and the clubs officials are : Messrs. E. Gleaye (treasurer), and G. N. Rigby (sec.). So far as I can understand,' there will be no steam launches runnifs.• from Widnes behind the boats, for tho the accommodation of spectators.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the above was held on Tuesday, at the Horsemarket-st. CocoaTuoms,there being a good attendance of delegates. A c@mmuni- cation was read from the Pailiarnentsry Commit- tee of the Trades Union Congress, urging the Coun- cil send delegates to the Conference which is be- ing held to-day (Saturday), in London, in reference to the Employers' Liability Bill. The Council could not, however, see its way to send representatives. The Associated Iron and Steel Workers or Great Britain and Ireland, of which there are several branches in Warrington, will be represented by their General Sfeerctaries,as will also the Am algam- ated Society of 'ail way Servants. whose members of the Warrington branch are affiliated with the Council They desire it to be stated that althoueh it is alleged that the voluntary Association which exists !between the railway companies and their servants would be destroyed if the Bill came into force, as it stood they do not believe that such results would fellow from the passing of the Bill, and the position of their organisation has been strenu- ously in opposition to contracting out the railway men, therefore, placing themselves on an equality with their fellow trades unions of the country in respect to this clause in the Bill. The delegates to the Hairdressers' Association expressed their gratitude to the Council for the assistance rendered to them in the endeavour to maintain the rules of their organisation and hal! holiday movement, and stated that they will take further action later on in thosea,son. A settlement was made by the Coopers' delegates,with reference to the Coopers applying for admission into the Navy at the age of 18. The Cooners are of opinion that the age should be altered to 21,as the Government are aiding apprentices to break the law by which they are hound. ThQ following resolu- tion was unanimously passed on the motion of the , Coopers' delegates, copies of which will be forwarded to the Admiralty, Parliamentary Committeeof the Trades Union Congress, and all members of Parliament who would be likely to interest themselves in the matter : " That this Council views with much concern the action of the Government in advertising for Coopers at the are of from 18 to 25 years, and asks them to amend this by substittiting—that in future all applicants must satisfy their recruiting officer that they are properly qualified Coopers, by producing their indentures of apprentice- ship, or some other sufficient guarantee of skill and effi- ri.rwv for the duties they are called upon to perform."

div.p: ELLESMERE-STREET MISSION BAZAAR,
WARRINGTON.

A bazaar was opened in the Bold-st., Wesleyan schoolroom on Wednesday, in aid of the Ellesmere- at. Mission, which commenced its existence twelve months ago, and which has still a debt of over £2OO remaining upon it. The bazaar was opened by Mr. E.J. Guest, J.P., and there were also present at the opening ceremony, the Revs. J. Kirtlan, Owen Wat- kins, G. D. Mason, and J. Gunnell, Mrs. Gunnell, Dr. and Miss. Gornall, Mr. and Mrs. C. E. Parker,Mr. R. G. Henshall, Mr. Winstanley, Mr. W. Brough,Mr. W. C. Nicholson, Miss Smith, Mrs. Holford, Mr. L. Richardson (superintendent.), and Mr. I. E. Barlow (secret ary). Before the opening of the bazaar, the Rev. J. Kirtlan , gave a short accoent of the scheme which resulted in the buiiding of Ellesinere-st. Mission. He said that when Bold-st.schools were erected,there was another building in Buthermarket-st.,whi-li was on sale but they could not sell it, and some of the mission workers of Bold-st. asked to be allowed to use it for mission services. This per- , mission was granted by the trustees, and work was carried on for a number of years ; and good work was being dene. Just as he (Mr. Kirtlan) came into the circuit, the Fate was completed, and in a short tirne, the inissi..n workers had notice to quit. They had a good conaregation, and there were over 200 young people in the Sueday school, and there was no place to go to except in the street. They tried in all the district for some p!ace, but could not get any room, nor anywhere to worship in. Alter a great deal of consideration they decided upon the present site in Ellesmere-at. for a new mission place, and they opened it under very favoura ble circumstances twelve months ago. If they could place on a diagram b the work which was being done, and the success oesl that work during the last twelve months, he was quite sure it would cheer the hearts of those present, as the work had been most successful. They had a Sun- day School in Ellesmere-st., with over 300 children, and he did not think that anyone %could employ themselves better on a Sunday afternoon than occasionally going down there to See what was being done in the neighbour- hood where so much was required. He was glad to say that there were about 50 young men attending the school. There was also a large congregation, and there was a large programme of social work being carried on during winter. He was sure that it would be interesting to know what they were doing. On Monday, they had a class to teach writing, and after that a society class meeting. On Tuaiday they taught reading. On Wednesday there was a Band of Hope. On Thursday there was an arithmetic class and a shorthand class. On Friday there was a boy's brigade and recreation class, and on Saturday afternoon was a penny bank in a very flourishing condition and on Saturday evening were penny concerts. He did not think there was any part in the circuit where the pre- mises had been better used. There was about 60 or 70 members who met in the society class. The amount of building the iron chapel was £2BB, and with other ex- penses it amounted to £323. The trustees of the other property agreed to give £5O to the scheme and at the opening services they obtained £4O, which made £9O with which to start, and there was, therefore, a deficit of 238 to clear, tie did not know whether they could clear that sum at the present bazaar, but he hoped that a large share would be cleared, as it was absolutely necessary that the debt should be cleared off. He was sorry that Mr. J. B. Isaac could not be present,as it was due to him in conjunction with Messrs. Dale, W. Brough and J. Hartioy, that they were able to build the build- ing, as they came forward and offered to be surety for the _money. .

Mr. E. J. GUEST, J.P., said that the honours of this life were often unequally distributed, and he thought that the honour of opening the bazaar should have fallen upon one of the four gentlemen who had done so much for the mission. He however had great love for the work of God, and a desire for the extension of His kingdom, especially in this town. (Applause). And he thought that there was no organisation which was equal to the Chris- tian Church for promoting the good of the people. He did not believe in multiplying sects, but he rejoiced that a large and influential church like the Methodist church in Warrington was sending out its branches for the spread of the gospel. He was pleased to think that they had a mission in Ellesmere-tit. and he believed that it would be productive of great good. He looked forward in the future to seeing the mission grow iato a great and powerful church. (Applause.) He was glad that it was connected with Bold-st. chapel, as he had a deep love for that place. His father was deeply interested in the chapel and he was there at the commencement. He helped to build it, and had taken great interest in the chapel for 29 years. Even when he became deaf he stood in the aisle and extended the right hand of fellowship to B:rangers. (Applause.) It was in connection with Bold-st. that he (the speaker) first heard the gospel and where he made his first public acknowledgment of allegiance to the Lord Jesus Christ. He was sorry that they sold Buttermareet-st. schools, but perhaps they had ample reasons for going to Ellestnere-st., as it was more in the centre of population. He was a believer in bazaars. They were a gooi means of getting money,and although articles might be a little higher in price than elsewhere, still it was for. a good cause. He thought something was due to those who had spent their time in working for the present bazaar. He had great pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. The Rev.Owee WATKINB,iII proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Guest, said that he looked upon Ellesmere st. as practically a new departure. Methodism was the church of the masses,and when the Methodists forgot the masses may God forget them. He rejoiced greatly in the self sacrificing, earnest work which their friends at Ellesmere at. had been doing during the past year. .The mission was a child of Botil-at., and Bold-st.ought to be proud of it. He looked forward to the time when a large church, perhaps a little further away from Bold-street, would be built.as this was the legitimate outgrowth of the work of the mission. There would be great changes of popula- tion in the near future of which Warrington would be the centre. Who could tell what effect the Manchester Ship Canal would have upon these changes? He need not be a prophet to say that the population of War- rington would be greatly affected, and that especially when the docks were made. It was the duty of the church to prepare for the multitudes of the people who would come to live in their midst. He rejoiced to see Mr. Guest there that day, and thanked him for opening the bazaar,and it would give him great pleasure in mov- ine• a vote of thanks to him.

Dr. GORNALL seconded the vote of thanks. He said that Mr. Guest esteemed it the greatest honour of his life to promote what he believed to be true religion. Tho motion was carried unanimously, and Mr. GUIST briefly replied. The room presented a pretty appearance. There were ranged around it six stalls all draped in art muslin. The first was the Forget-me-not Stall, draped in blue and green muslin. The articles were chiefly fany ware,such as plaques,dolls,hc. Conspicuous on the stall was a fine framed portrait of the Right Hon.W. E. Gladstone,M.P., ex-Premier, which was given by Mrs. John Crosfield. The stall holders were :—Mrs. Mason, Mrs. Isaac E. Barlow. and Mrs. Davenport. The next was the Wild Rose stall, draped in green and uink. The articles were chiefly fancy vases and similar articles. The stall holders were Mrs. Watkins, Mrs. Nicholson and Mrs. Jowett. The Daffodil stall was under the charge of Mrs. Kirtlan, Mrs. Barlow, Mrs. John Ellison and Mrs. Greg- son. It was draped with yellow and green muslin, and the articles were similar to the Wild Rose stall. Next in order was the Flower stall, draped in pink and green, under the charge of Miss A.Gornall and Miss Hartley,and on which was a large quantity of beautiful flowers. The Daisy stall came nest, and it contained a large assort- ment of fancy goods, such as needlework, D'Oyleys, pincushions, purses, and other knick-knacks. It was I draped in yellow and white muslin, and was under the care of Miss haac, Miss Doncaster and Miss E. Sherlock. This was the Sundae. SAtool stall. Next followed the refreshment stall under the name of the Ivy stall.draned in red and green, under the charge of Miss Barlow, Miss Roff, Miss K. Roll, Miss Gaukroeer and Miss N. Ash- worth. Over all the stalls were flowers corresponding to the names of the stalls. There was also a tea-room tinder the superintendence 6f Mrs, Lingard. In addi- tion to these, there were the usual adjuncts to a bazaar There was a museum and art gallery in which Mr. W. J. Ashton acted as conductor. Mr. Gilbert Carter had charge of a shooting gallery. There were also vestries in which there was an optical lantern tinder tho charge of Professor Podsnap, and a shadowgraph in which "'Pro- fessor Fang" was the presiding genius. "Professor Max Millar " felt the bumps of all who wished to know their own character. Mr. W. A. Mellor had under his charge a panorama. The decorations reflected great credit upon Mr. W. C. Nicholson who superintended them. Mr. Levi Richardson had charge of the enter- taintnonts and all the musical items.

In the evening, there was a large number present,:and the various vestries were well patronised,especiallv that of Professor Max Millar, who did good business in his delineation of character. The amount realised for the day was £5O.

div.head: SECOND DAY.
div.p: SECOND DAY.

On Thursday, the bazaar was opened by Mr. H. G. Henshall, who said that it gave him great pleasure to hp present that afternoon. He Supposed that a eirruit steward was always expected to be reaJv at a moment's notice for anything, and he could not refuse to con. when he was asked to do so. He had listened with great interest to Mr. Kirtlan's remarks the previous clay, when he described the various agencies for educational ;yid evangelistic work which were being carried 071 111 the Mission at Ellesmere-st., and he was sure that in their works of faith and labours of love, they had the t•yin- pathy of all the members of the Wesleyan congregations in Warrington. They all knew and valued the work they were doing. He was glad that they had hail a fair mea- sure of success the previous day aria he hoped that they would be equally successful that day. The Rev. G. D. MA.sox in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Henshall, paid a tribute to the laity of the circuit for their co-operation with the ministers, and for their assistance in their work. Ho hoped to see in Ellesmere- st.Mission a flourishing church which would be the centre of activity in the town and neighbourhood. The Rev. OWEN WATRINS seconded and the Rev. J.

On Wednesday evening, the boa brigade in connec- tion with the mission gave the two choruses, C9airo join the volunteers," " Onward Christian Soldiers," and a dumbbell performance in an efficient manner, tna,'er the leadership of Sergeant A,lvvorta, the accompanist being Mr. Charles Broadhurst. div.head: MEETING OF THE COMMITTEE.
div.p: MEETING OF THE COMMITTEE.

The inquiry ir.to the proposal of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners to divide the town into wards took place yesterday afternoon at the Town Hall, Runcorn, toe cirlic being taken by Dr. lloilgeon, who was accompanied by the retnaining two reresentati twes appointed by the Cheshire ' County Council, Mr. John If.vaus, and Mr. Philip Spas-1k man. There were. also present Messrs. E. Imison, tV Hatullev, J. Nleerlowcreft, J. ‘r. Light- burn. B. Kniveton, W. Sutton, A. IL Norman,J. Lee, H. White, A. L glitburn, Handley, J. Wiihaws, J Moss,and Dr. McKei,z,e, with the law clerk, Mr. F. A. Lake ; sec- retary, Mr. E. Marshall ; surveyor, Mr. M. Barker ; and the assistant surveyor, Mr. J. Wilding. After the tonnat opening had taken place the Chairman asked if anyore, was present to raise objection to the scheme, whereupon Mr. Lightburn intimated that he individually- was opposed to the division of the town int* wards. Mr. Lake first of all stated that the petition which had already been published should be taken as read. He then proceeded to describethe boundaries of the six wards which are to be called Halton ward, Alitreey ward, Cen- tral ward, Bridgewater ward, Newton ward, and Heath ward. He intimated the number of houses, electorsond rateable value of each. Be went on to state that the petition was adopted by eight to seven at a meeting of the Commissioners on January 4th. Subsequently he called upan Mr. Marshall to confirm the paseine of a minute and the due sealing of the petition which was forwarded to the County Council. Mr. Lightburn was then asked to state his objections which he said numbered three. It first of all robbed the ratepayers of five-sixths of their representation. He con- sidered that Runcorn was so small that the Commis- sioners were able to have an oversight of the whole. town. Then, secondly, the division into wards might possibly leave a chance for men of inferior standing to be placed upon the Board. He stated that the chief argument in favour of the scheme was the increased facility it would give for electors recording their votes. In answer to the Chairman he said he had no opposition to the proposed boundaries. The Chairman remarked that the opposition was rather unique, inasmuch as it was the desire of all Urban Authorities to ne divided into wards so that repre- sentation might be more centralised. The County Conn- . cil had had applications from various places, and even in some instances where wards already existed, they were desirous of these being increased, and thereby focus the district into a more limited area. Mr. Meadowcroft opposed on the ground that it would considerably increase the cost of elections with- out getting any material corresponding advantage. The. question of boundaries submitted was new to him and the public, and consequently he had no alternative scheme to present. He thought the ratepayers had bees well served in the past, and that the prot.o3ed division into wards would in no way improve matters. The ex- pense of administration would be considerably in- creased, whereas they would get no benefr. Mr. Handley and Mr. fraison conteneted that the sub- ject had been fully before the C'oinmissi.oners previous to the petition being forwarded to the Coumy Council. The Chairman said they would have to report to the County Council the result of the inquiry,. and it would be for them to decide wiletlier they would grant the praer of the oetitionere or otherwise. He said that the general basis of dividieg the town had been adapted, namely, by making those dietricts where there was no prospect of extension to cover the striaileet area and to leave r,,orte for the elements or growth in those where the elecNrate was the smallest.
On the motitm of Mr. Lightburn, seconded by Mr. Handley, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman for presiding.

COUNTY OF CHESTER. CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 AND 1886. CLEANSING AND DISINFECTION OF MARKETS, FAIRS, SALEYARDS, PLACES OF EXHIBITION, OR OTHER PLACES USED FOR ANIMALS. NTOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Executive Committee of the Local Authority of this County, at a Meeting held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on Thursday, the Ist day of March, 1894. ORDERED—That the existing Regulations made on the 30th day of June, 1834, as to the Cleansing and Nisinfection pf Markets, Fairs, Saleyards, Places of Exhibition, or other Places used for Animals, should be amended by providing that the Owners, Lessees, or Occupiers of such Markets, Fairs, Saleyards, Places of Exhibition. kc., should Cleanse and Disinfect the same to the satisfaction of the Inspector for the District, within 48 hours from the conclusion of such Market, Fair, Sale, or Exhibition of Animals, &c., such Cleansing and Disinfection being carried out in the following manner, viz :- 1. By the sweeping out and effectually removing all dung, sawdust, litter, and other matter. 2. By the thorough cleansing thereof with water. 3. And if and when required by an Inspector, all parts of such places used as before-mentioned shall be well sprinkled over with a solution of 'carbolic acid and water, in the following proportions, viz., half-a-pint of corbolic acid well mixed with each gallon of water. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Cheshire County Council. Chester, Ist March, 1894.
